<result>=== lib/memory/call-lifecycle.ts
// Memory lifecycle for one SDK conversation hook: recall at begin, inject at
// connect, ingest at disconnect. Plain class (no React), so the restart
// orderings can be exercised directly; use-elevenlabs-memory.ts wraps it.
//
// The SDK's connect/disconnect callbacks carry no attempt, and on a language
// change the old session's onDisconnect can land after begin() has armed the
// new call. So this never ends "the current call". Each connect opens a
// conversation, and each disconnect retires the oldest open one: sessions on a
// single SDK hook close in the order they opened. A late disconnect therefore
// ingests the old call and leaves the new one alone.
//
// begin() also takes an attempt token, so a recall from a replaced call never
// reaches the new one. Each conversation ingests at most once.
//
// A call may also carry a preface (a resumed conversation, see
// lib/conversations/resume.ts). It goes out at connect, ahead of the memories,
// whether or not memory is on. With memory off, the call neither recalls nor
// ingests.

import type { Lang } from "@/lib/lang";
import type { IngestTarget } from "./client";

export interface LifecycleDeps {
  userId: () => string;
  recall: (userId: string) => Promise<string[]>;
  format: (memories: string[], lang: Lang) => string | null;
  ingest: (target: IngestTarget) => void;
}

export interface BeginOptions {
  /** Recall before and ingest after this call (the memory.recall tool). */
  memory: boolean;
  /** Context to send first at connect, e.g. an earlier conversation being continued. */
  preface?: string | null;
}

interface CallRecord {
  attempt: number;
  userId: string;
  persona?: string;
  lang: Lang;
  memory: boolean;
  preface: string | null;
  recall: Promise<string[]>;
  injecting?: boolean;
}

const NO_MEMORIES: Promise<string[]> = Promise.resolve([]);

export class MemoryCallLifecycle {
  private attempt = 0;
  /** The call armed by the latest begin(); recall is injected only into it. */
  private current: CallRecord | null = null;
  /** Connected conversations not yet disconnected, oldest first. */
  private open: { id: string; call: CallRecord }[] = [];
  private ingested = new Set<string>();

  constructor(private readonly deps: LifecycleDeps) {}

  /** CALL pressed: start recall in parallel with connecting. Returns the session userId. */
  begin(
    persona: string | undefined,
    lang: Lang,
    { memory, preface = null }: BeginOptions = { memory: true },
  ): string {
    const userId = this.deps.userId();
    this.current = {
      attempt: ++this.attempt,
      userId,
      persona,
      lang,
      memory,
      preface,
      recall: memory ? this.deps.recall(userId) : NO_MEMORIES,
    };
    return userId;
  }

  /** onConnect: open the conversation, then send its preface and recalled memories once. */
  connected(conversationId: string, send: (text: string) => void): void {
    const call = this.current;
    if (!call) return;
    this.open.push({ id: conversationId, call });
    if (call.injecting) return;
    call.injecting = true;
    const { attempt } = call;
    if (call.preface) trySend(send, call.preface);
    if (!call.memory) return;
    void call.recall.then((memories) => {
      if (this.attempt !== attempt || this.current !== call) return;
      const text = this.deps.format(memories, call.lang);
      if (text) trySend(send, text);
    });
  }

  /** onDisconnect: ingest the oldest open conversation. */
  ended(): void {
    const open = this.open.shift();
    if (!open) return;
    // A recall still in flight for this call has nothing left to reach.
    if (this.current === open.call) this.current = null;
    if (!open.call.memory || this.ingested.has(open.id)) return;
    this.ingested.add(open.id);
    this.deps.ingest({
      userId: open.call.userId,
      conversationId: open.id,
      persona: open.call.persona,
      lang: open.call.lang,
    });
  }
}

function trySend(send: (text: string) => void, text: string): void {
  try {
    send(text);
  } catch {
    // The call ended before the update could go out; nothing to inject.
  }
}

=== lib/memory/mem0-rest.ts
// Server-only mem0 Platform REST helpers (v3), used by app/api/memory/*.
//
// Plain fetch instead of the mem0ai SDK, matching the other provider routes.
// Memory is scoped by user_id only: mem0 stores entities separately, so an AND
// of user_id + agent_id returns nothing. Persona, language and source live in
// metadata instead, which also keeps one memory shared by all seven aspects.

const MEM0_BASE = "https://api.mem0.ai";

export interface Mem0Message {
  role: "user" | "assistant";
  content: string;
}

export interface Mem0Memory {
  id: string;
  memory: string;
  metadata?: Record<string, unknown> | null;
  created_at?: string;
  updated_at?: string;
}

export class Mem0Error extends Error {
  constructor(
    message: string,
    readonly status: number,
  ) {
    super(message);
  }
}

export function mem0ApiKey(): string | undefined {
  return process.env.MEM0_API_KEY || undefined;
}

async function mem0Post<T>(apiKey: string, path: string, body: unknown): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(MEM0_BASE + path, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Token ${apiKey}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
    cache: "no-store",
  });
  const text = await res.text();
  if (!res.ok) throw new Mem0Error(`mem0 ${path} failed: ${text.slice(0, 300)}`, res.status);
  return (text ? JSON.parse(text) : {}) as T;
}

/**
 * Queue a conversation for fact extraction. mem0 processes it asynchronously.
 * `timestamp` (Unix seconds) dates the memories to when the call happened rather
 * than when ingest ran, which is when mem0 would otherwise anchor "this Friday".
 */
export async function addMemories(
  apiKey: string,
  userId: string,
  messages: Mem0Message[],
  metadata: Record<string, string>,
  timestamp?: number,
): Promise<{ event_id?: string; status?: string }> {
  return mem0Post(apiKey, "/v3/memories/add/", {
    user_id: userId,
    messages,
    metadata,
    ...(timestamp ? { timestamp } : {}),
  });
}

// mem0 doesn't document get-all ordering, so the newest memories can sit on any
// page. Read every page (while mem0 reports a `next`), then sort locally. The cap
// bounds recall latency for a very long-lived visitor at 1,000 memories.
const LIST_PAGE_SIZE = 100;
const LIST_MAX_PAGES = 10;

interface Mem0Page {
  results?: Mem0Memory[];
  next?: string | null;
}

/** The user's most recently updated memories, newest first. */
export async function listRecentMemories(
  apiKey: string,
  userId: string,
  limit: number,
): Promise<Mem0Memory[]> {
  const all: Mem0Memory[] = [];
  for (let page = 1; page <= LIST_MAX_PAGES; page++) {
    const res = await mem0Post<Mem0Page>(
      apiKey,
      `/v3/memories/?page=${page}&page_size=${LIST_PAGE_SIZE}`,
      { filters: { user_id: userId } },
    );
    all.push(...(res.results ?? []));
    if (!res.next || !res.results?.length) break;
  }
  const stamp = (m: Mem0Memory) => Date.parse(m.updated_at ?? m.created_at ?? "") || 0;
  return all.sort((a, b) => stamp(b) - stamp(a)).slice(0, limit);
}

=== app/api/memory/ingest/route.ts
// Post-call ingest: feed a finished ElevenLabs conversation into mem0.
//
// The browser posts the conversation id it captured at connect. The transcript
// itself comes from ElevenLabs (already stored there), not from the browser,
// and the call must belong to the posting visitor: the session is started with
// that `userId`, and ElevenLabs records it on the conversation.
//
// Ingest runs at most once per (visitor, conversation) in this server process.
// The reservation is keyed by both, so a refused request for someone else's call
// can never mark that call as done for its real owner. mem0 also merges facts it
// has already extracted, so a repeat after a server restart is harmless.
//
// Dev only: MEM0_API_KEY and ELEVENLABS_API_KEY come from fnox.

import {
  ConversationError,
  fetchFinishedConversation,
  toMem0Messages,
} from "@/lib/memory/elevenlabs-conversation";
import { isConversationId, isMemoryUserId } from "@/lib/memory/ids";
import { Mem0Error, addMemories, mem0ApiKey } from "@/lib/memory/mem0-rest";
import { LANGS, type Lang } from "@/lib/lang";

export const runtime = "nodejs";
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";

const PERSONA_ID_RE = /^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$/;
const ingested = new Set<string>();

interface IngestRequest {
  userId?: unknown;
  conversationId?: unknown;
  persona?: unknown;
  lang?: unknown;
}

function fail(error: string, status: number): Response {
  return Response.json({ error }, { status });
}

export async function POST(req: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const mem0Key = mem0ApiKey();
  if (!mem0Key) return fail("MEM0_API_KEY is not set on the server.", 503);
  const elevenKey = process.env.ELEVENLABS_API_KEY;
  if (!elevenKey) return fail("ELEVENLABS_API_KEY is not set on the server.", 503);

  let body: IngestRequest;
  try {
    body = (await req.json()) as IngestRequest;
  } catch {
    return fail("Invalid JSON body.", 400);
  }
  const { userId, conversationId, persona, lang } = body;
  if (!isMemoryUserId(userId)) return fail("userId is missing or malformed.", 400);
  if (!isConversationId(conversationId)) return fail("conversationId is malformed.", 400);
  const personaId = typeof persona === "string" && PERSONA_ID_RE.test(persona) ? persona : "";
  const sessionLang: Lang = LANGS.includes(lang as Lang) ? (lang as Lang) : "en";

  const key = `${userId}:${conversationId}`;
  if (ingested.has(key)) return Response.json({ status: "duplicate" });
  ingested.add(key);

  try {
    const conv = await fetchFinishedConversation(elevenKey, conversationId);
    if (conv.user_id !== userId) {
      ingested.delete(key);
      return fail("conversation does not belong to this visitor.", 403);
    }
    const messages = toMem0Messages(conv);
    if (!messages.some((m) => m.role === "user")) {
      return Response.json({ status: "skipped", reason: "no user turns" });
    }
    const event = await addMemories(
      mem0Key,
      userId,
      messages,
      {
        source: "elevenlabs",
        conversation_id: conversationId,
        agent: conv.agent_name ?? "",
        persona: personaId,
        lang: sessionLang,
      },
      conv.metadata?.start_time_unix_secs,
    );
    return Response.json({ status: "queued", turns: messages.length, event_id: event.event_id });
  } catch (err) {
    // Let a later attempt retry a call that failed upstream.
    ingested.delete(key);
    const status = err instanceof ConversationError || err instanceof Mem0Error ? err.status : 502;
    const message = err instanceof Error ? err.message : "network error";
    return fail(message, status >= 400 && status < 600 ? status : 502);
  }
}

=== app/api/memory/recall/route.ts
// Pre-call recall: the visitor's most recent mem0 memories, shared by all personas.
//
// The browser calls this when CALL is pressed, in parallel with connecting, and
// hands the result to the agent as a contextual update once the call is up.
// Listing beats searching here: before the first utterance there is no query,
// and a broad "who is this person" search scores barely above mem0's threshold.
//
// Dev only: MEM0_API_KEY comes from fnox (`fnox exec -- bun run dev`). Without
// it the route answers 503 and the call simply proceeds without memory.

import { isMemoryUserId } from "@/lib/memory/ids";
import { Mem0Error, listRecentMemories, mem0ApiKey } from "@/lib/memory/mem0-rest";

export const runtime = "nodejs";
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";

const RECALL_LIMIT = 20;

export async function POST(req: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const apiKey = REDACTED;
  if (!apiKey) {
    return Response.json({ error: "MEM0_API_KEY is not set on the server." }, { status: 503 });
  }

  let userId: unknown;
  try {
    ({ userId } = (await req.json()) as { userId?: unknown });
  } catch {
    return Response.json({ error: "Invalid JSON body." }, { status: 400 });
  }
  if (!isMemoryUserId(userId)) {
    return Response.json({ error: "userId is missing or malformed." }, { status: 400 });
  }

  try {
    const memories = await listRecentMemories(apiKey, userId, RECALL_LIMIT);
    return Response.json(
      { memories: memories.map((m) => m.memory).filter(Boolean) },
      { headers: { "Cache-Control": "no-store" } },
    );
  } catch (err) {
    const status = err instanceof Mem0Error ? err.status : 0;
    const message = err instanceof Error ? err.message : "network error";
    return Response.json({ error: message, status }, { status: 502 });
  }
}

=== lib/conversations/resume.ts
// How an earlier call is handed back to the persona when the visitor continues it.
//
// Sent as an ElevenLabs contextual update at connect, like recalled memories.
// It stays in-world: the spirit picks the conversation back up. It never says
// "transcript" or "log", and it never reads the old lines back.

import type { Lang } from "@/lib/lang";
import type { ConversationTurn } from "./types";

/** What a resume needs: the earlier turns, and their language (it may differ from the session's). */
export interface ResumeSource {
  lang: Lang;
  transcript: ConversationTurn[];
}

// The tail of a long call carries the thread; the beginning is mostly greetings.
// The bound keeps the update well inside the agent's context on a long call.
export const RESUME_MAX_TURNS = 40;
const RESUME_MAX_CHARS_PER_TURN = 600;

const FRAMING: Record<
  Lang,
  { head: string; you: string; them: string; rules: string[]; otherLang: string }
> = {
  en: {
    head: "You are picking up an earlier conversation with the person you are speaking with. This is how it went, oldest first:",
    you: "You",
    them: "Them",
    rules: [
      "Carry on from where it stopped, as someone returning to an unfinished conversation, not meeting them for the first time.",
      "Never read the earlier lines back, and never mention a transcript, a log, or any system.",
    ],
    otherLang: "The earlier conversation was in Japanese. Keep speaking English.",
  },
  ja: {
    head: "いま話している相手との、以前の会話の続きをするところです。そのときのやり取りは次のとおり（古い順）：",
    you: "あなた",
    them: "相手",
    rules: [
      "初対面としてではなく、途中だった会話に戻ってきた者として、止まったところから続けること。",
      "以前のやり取りを読み上げないこと。記録、ログ、仕組みのことには決して触れないこと。",
    ],
    otherLang: "以前の会話は英語だったが、話すのは日本語のままにすること。",
  },
};

function clip(text: string): string {
  return text.length > RESUME_MAX_CHARS_PER_TURN
    ? `${text.slice(0, RESUME_MAX_CHARS_PER_TURN)}…`
    : text;
}

/** The contextual-update text that resumes `source` in a `lang` session, or null if it has no turns. */
export function formatResumeUpdate(source: ResumeSource, lang: Lang): string | null {
  const turns = source.transcript.slice(-RESUME_MAX_TURNS);
  if (turns.length === 0) return null;
  const f = FRAMING[lang];
  const lines = turns.map((t) => `${t.who === "agent" ? f.you : f.them}: ${clip(t.text)}`);
  const rules = source.lang === lang ? f.rules : [...f.rules, f.otherLang];
  return [f.head, ...lines, "", ...rules].join("\n");
}

=== lib/memory/framing.ts
// How recalled memories are handed to the persona, in the session's language.
//
// Sent as an ElevenLabs contextual update, which the agent reads as background,
// not as a user turn. The framing stays in-world: the spirit simply remembers
// the visitor. It must never talk about notes, records or a memory system, and
// it never recites the list. Memories may be written in either language (a
// Japanese call yields Japanese facts), so the rule says to speak the session's
// language regardless.

import type { Lang } from "@/lib/lang";

const FRAMING: Record<Lang, { head: string; rules: string[] }> = {
  en: {
    head: "What you remember about the person you are speaking with, from earlier conversations with you or with another of your aspects:",
    rules: [
      "Bring a memory in only when it fits the moment. Never list them or recite them back.",
      "Speak as someone who simply remembers. Never mention notes, records, or any system.",
      "If something seems out of date, let them correct you and go with what they say now.",
      "Some memories may be written in Japanese. Keep speaking English.",
    ],
  },
  ja: {
    head: "いま話している相手について、あなた自身、またはあなたの別の相との以前の会話から覚えていること：",
    rules: [
      "思い出は、その場に自然に合うときだけ持ち出すこと。一覧にしたり、読み上げたりしないこと。",
      "ただ覚えている者として話すこと。メモ、記録、仕組みのことには決して触れないこと。",
      "古くなっていそうなことは相手に正してもらい、いま相手が言うことに従うこと。",
      "英語で書かれた思い出もあるが、話すのは日本語のままにすること。",
    ],
  },
};

/** The contextual-update text for these memories, or null when there is nothing to send. */
export function formatMemoryUpdate(memories: string[], lang: Lang): string | null {
  if (memories.length === 0) return null;
  const { head, rules } = FRAMING[lang];
  return [head, ...memories.map((m) => `- ${m}`), "", ...rules].join("\n");
}

=== app/api/openai/token/route.ts
// Mints a short-lived OpenAI realtime ephemeral key (client secret) server-side
// so the browser can open a WebRTC session WITHOUT ever seeing OPENAI_API_KEY.
//
// Flow: client POSTs here → we call OpenAI with the secret key → return the
// ephemeral key JSON. The browser then negotiates WebRTC directly with OpenAI:
//   POST https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls
//     Authorization: Bearer <ephemeral key>, Content-Type: application/sdp

export async function POST(): Promise<Response> {
  const apiKey = process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) {
    // Do not echo any key material; just say it's unset.
    return Response.json(
      { error: "OPENAI_API_KEY is not set on the server (provide it via fnox)." },
      { status: 500 },
    );
  }

  let upstream: Response;
  try {
    upstream = await fetch(CLIENT_SECRETS_URL, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ session: { type: "realtime", model: OPENAI_REALTIME_MODEL } }),
    });
  } catch (err) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: `Failed to reach OpenAI: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : "network error"}` },
      { status: 502 },
    );
  }

  const text = await upstream.text();
  if (!upstream.ok) {
    // Surface OpenAI's status + body (it doesn't contain our key) for debugging.
    return Response.json(
      { error: "OpenAI client_secrets request failed", status: upstream.status, detail: text },
      { status: 502 },
    );
  }

  // Pass the key JSON straight through; the client extracts the value defensively.
  return new Response(text, {
    status: 200,
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Cache-Control": "no-store" },
  });
}

// Japanese for the prompt-level engines (xAI Grok Voice, OpenAI Realtime,
// Gemini Live native audio).
//
// None of these sessions has a language parameter — the model follows the
// instructions and the opening turn. So a Japanese session is the same persona
// (same voice, same English persona prompt) with two changes:
//   1. a language rule appended to the instructions, and
//   2. the opening direction swapped for one that elicits the persona's
//      Japanese greeting.
// (OpenAI additionally takes a transcription language hint — see openai-agent.ts.)
//
// ElevenLabs does NOT go through here: it routes Japanese to a dedicated JA
// agent with its own JA prompt and cast voice (elevenlabs-agent.ts).

import { PERSONAS } from "@/lib/data";
import type { Lang } from "@/lib/lang";

/** The slice of an engine's agent config that carries language. */
interface Localizable {
  instructions: string;
  firstMessage: string;
}

function languageRule(jaName?: string): string {
  const name = jaName ? ` Say your own name in its Japanese form, ${jaName}.` : "";
  return (
    "Language: always converse in natural spoken Japanese (日本語), even though these " +
    "instructions are written in English. Keep replying in Japanese if the user speaks " +
    "another language, unless they explicitly ask you to switch. Match the user's level of " +
    "politeness." +
    name
  );
}

// The engines elicit their opening from a user-side direction (never a
// scripted assistant turn), so the greeting is requested, not injected.
function greetingDirection(greet?: string): string {
  return greet
    ? `Open in Japanese. Say this greeting word for word, then wait for my reply: 「${greet}」`
    : "Greet me briefly in Japanese as a calm aspect of the ancient camellia spirit and ask how you can help.";
}

/**
 * Apply the session language to a resolved agent config. English is the
 * identity; Japanese appends the language rule and swaps the opening direction.
 */
export function localizeAgent<T extends Localizable>(
  agent: T,
  personaId: string | undefined,
  lang: Lang,
): T {
  if (lang !== "ja") return agent;
  const ja = PERSONAS.find((p) => p.id === personaId)?.ja;
  return {
    ...agent,
    instructions: `${agent.instructions}\n\n${languageRule(ja?.name)}`,
    firstMessage: greetingDirection(ja?.greet),
  };
}

            if (stateRef.current === "interrupted") setCallState("listening");
            break;
          case "output_audio_buffer.started":
            // Agent audio is now playing (WebRTC-only event). With barge-in off,
            // go half-duplex: silence the mic so speaker leak can't be committed
            // as a user turn and answered. With barge-in on, the mic stays open
            // so the user can talk over the agent.
            if (!bargeInRef.current) setMicGated(true);
            break;
          case "output_audio_buffer.stopped":
          case "output_audio_buffer.cleared":
            // Playback drained (or was cleared by interrupt) — reopen the mic.
            // Gate off here rather than at response.done: generation finishes
            // while the audio tail is still playing, and that tail is the echo.
            setMicGated(false);
            break;
          case "conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.delta":
            if (msg.delta) pushUserDelta(msg.delta);
            break;
          case "conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed":
            finalizeUser(msg.transcript ?? "");
            break;
          // ── Remote MCP tools (executed by the Realtime API, not by us) ──
          case "mcp_list_tools.failed":
            // Tools didn't import; the call continues voice-only.
            console.warn("[openai] firecrawl MCP tool listing failed");
            break;
          case "response.mcp_call.in_progress":
            // The model is between speech segments while the tool runs, so the
            // caption is free — surface the activity instead of dead air.
            setCaption("searching the web…");
            break;
          case "response.mcp_call.failed":
            setCaption("— web tool call failed —");
            break;
          case "conversation.item.done":
            // Defensive: our firecrawl config is require_approval "never", but
            // if the server ever asks anyway, auto-approve our own read-only
            // server rather than deadlocking the turn (an unanswered
            // mcp_approval_request stalls the tool call indefinitely).
            if (msg.item?.type === "mcp_approval_request") {
              if (msg.item.server_label === "firecrawl" && msg.item.id) {
                send({
                  type: "conversation.item.create",
                  item: {
                    type: "mcp_approval_response",
                    approval_request_id: msg.item.id,
                    approve: true,
                  },
                });
              } else {
                console.warn("[openai] unapproved MCP request from", msg.item.server_label);
              }
            }
            break;
          case "error":
            setCaption(`— ${msg.error?.message ?? "OpenAI error"} —`);
            break;
          default:
            break;
        }
      };

      // 5) Mint the ephemeral key, then exchange SDP with OpenAI.
      let token: string | null = null;
      try {
        const res = await fetch("/api/openai/token", { method: "POST" });
        const data = await res.json();
        if (!res.ok) {
          fail(`— ${typeof data?.error === "string" ? data.error : "token error"} —`);
          return;
        }
        token = extractToken(data);
      } catch {
        fail("— could not reach token endpoint —");
        return;
      }
      if (!token) {
        fail("— no OpenAI token returned —");
        return;
      }
      if (ended()) return;

      // Resolve Firecrawl access before the SDP exchange — the data channel
      // (whose open event triggers configure()) can't beat setRemoteDescription.
      const firecrawlAuth = await firecrawlAuthPromise;
      if (firecrawlAuth) tools = [firecrawlMcpTool(firecrawlAuth)];
      if (ended()) return;

      try {
        const offer = await pc.createOffer();
        await pc.setLocalDescription(offer);
        const sdpRes = await fetch(CALLS_URL, {
          method: "POST",
          body: offer.sdp,
          headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            "Content-Type": "application/sdp",
          },
        });
        if (!sdpRes.ok) {
          fail(`— OpenAI call setup failed (${await describeSetupFailure(sdpRes)}) —`);
          return;
        }
        const answer: RTCSessionDescriptionInit = { type: "answer", sdp: await sdpRes.text() };
        if (ended()) return;
        await pc.setRemoteDescription(answer);
      } catch {
        fail("— could not establish WebRTC session —");
        return;
      }
    })();
  }, [
    applyMicEnabled,
    beginAgentResponse,
    cancelAgentResponse,
    finalizeAgent,
    pushAgentDelta,
    send,
    setMicGated,
    teardown,
  ]);

  const stop = useCallback(() => {
    endedRef.current = true;
    teardown();
    setCallState("ended");
    setCaption("— call ended —");
  }, [teardown]);

  const interrupt = useCallback(() => {
    if (stateRef.current !== "speaking") return;
    // Cancel the in-progress response and clear any unplayed server audio.
    send({ type: "response.cancel" });
    send({ type: "output_audio_buffer.clear" });
    cancelAgentResponse();
    finalizeAgent();
    setCallState("interrupted");
    if (interruptTimerRef.current) clearTimeout(interruptTimerRef.current);
    interruptTimerRef.current = setTimeout(() => setCallState("listening"), 600);
  }, [cancelAgentResponse, finalizeAgent, send]);

  const setMuted = useCallback(
    (muted: boolean) => {
      mutedRef.current = muted;
      applyMicEnabled();
    },
    [applyMicEnabled],
  );

  const getInputVolume = useCallback(() => {
    if (mutedRef.current) return 0;
    return analyserLevel(inAnalyserRef.current, inBufRef.current);
  }, []);
  const getOutputVolume = useCallback(
    () => analyserLevel(outAnalyserRef.current, outBufRef.current),
    [],
  );

  // Reflect a barge-in toggle flip into a live session — `session.update` is a
  // merge, so only turn_detection needs resending. No-ops until configured
  // (send() drops messages while the data channel is closed).
  useEffect(() => {
    // Turning barge-in on mid-call lifts the half-duplex gate immediately —
    // don't leave the mic silenced waiting for the current playback to drain.
    if (bargeIn) setMicGated(false);
    if (!configuredRef.current) return;
    const agent = resolveOpenaiAgent(personaRef.current?.id, langRef.current);
    send({
      type: "session.update",
      session: {
        type: "realtime",
        audio: {
          input: {
            turn_detection: { ...agent.turnDetection, interrupt_response: bargeIn },
          },
        },
      },
    });
  }, [bargeIn, send, setMicGated]);

  // Hang up + reset if the provider is switched away from OpenAI mid-session.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (active) return;
    if (stateRef.current !== "idle") {
      endedRef.current = true;
      teardown();
      setCallState("idle");
      setTurns([]);
      setCaption("press CALL to begin");
    }
  }, [active, teardown]);

  // Cleanup on unmount.
  useEffect(() => () => teardown(), [teardown]);

  return useMemo<OpenaiSession>(
    () => ({
      callState,
      turns,
      caption,
      start,
      stop,
      interrupt,
      setMuted,
      getInputVolume,
      getOutputVolume,
    }),
    [callState, turns, caption, start, stop, interrupt, setMuted, getInputVolume, getOutputVolume],
  );
}

1. Add the message to `session.input` with `role: "developer"` and one `input_text` content part. See [Seed a session with prior conversation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#seed-a-session-with-prior-conversation) for the message format.

```

## Manage longer conversations

GPT-Live manages long conversations automatically and preserves your original startup instructions.

The default context window holds 128,000 tokens, including your instructions, conversation text, and audio tokens that don’t appear in the transcript.

GPT-Live summarizes older conversation history in the background. When context usage exceeds 90%, it starts a replacement voice engine within the same session. The replacement receives your original instructions and up to 8,192 tokens of conversation history, containing recent messages and, when available, a summary of older messages. Preparing a summary does not immediately change the running engine’s context.

Older conversation details may be summarized or omitted. Keep important facts, confirmed actions, and current task state in your application, and provide relevant context when needed.

## Store and fork a session

A fork starts a new session from a saved voice conversation. Use it to run several evaluation trials from the same reference conversation, or to let a user continue after an earlier session has ended. Each fork gets a new connection and session ID, with the source conversation and its saved configuration as its starting point.

### Run evaluations from a reference conversation

Suppose you want to test how your agent handles a caller changing an order. Record the setup once, through the point where the caller has identified the order. End and finalize that session before the caller asks to change it. Each evaluation can then fork the same reference session and receive the same next caller audio: “Actually, can you send it to my office instead?”

For each trial, restore the same test order and application state, supply the next caller input, and evaluate the new response and tool actions. You can repeat the scenario or compare supported Responses backend settings. Measure fork startup separately from response time. See the [GPT-Live evaluation guide](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation) for choosing scenarios and measuring results.

Forks inherit the GPT-Live model, voice, and original instructions. To compare a different voice model or startup prompt, create new sessions with that configuration. The fork API uses the completed source recording, so end the reference session where you want the evaluation to begin.

### Continue after a session ends

For example, a caller may hang up and call back later, or reconnect after a dropped call. If the earlier session has a completed stored recording, your application can fork it on a new connection and continue from the saved conversation.

Save application task state alongside the source session ID. Before continuing, check the status of any outstanding backend work and give the new session its current results. For example, if an order update was already submitted, confirm its outcome before attempting another update. Use the new session ID for controls and sideband connections, and route subsequent backend results to the new session.

### Prepare a session for forking

1. **Enable storage when you create the source.** Set `store: true` in its session configuration. Storage defaults to `false`, must be enabled for your project, and requires a data policy that permits persistence.
2. **Save the source session ID.** Read it from `session.started` or the WebRTC creation response, and associate it with your application’s conversation record.
3. **Finish and close the source.** Complete required backend work, then follow [Usage and graceful close](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#usage-and-graceful-close). Keep the connection open until `session.closed` and handle any finalization error. Forking requires a completed stored recording; saving it can add time to finalization.
4. **Start a fork on a new connection.** Use the source ID with the transport flow below, save the new session ID, and complete startup before continuing the conversation. Set the child’s `store` explicitly: `true` if you want to fork its continuation later, or `false` if you do not need to store that trial. Omitting it inherits the source setting.

See [GPT-Live data controls](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/data-residency#v1livesessions) for storage requirements.

For example, set this field in the source session’s WebSocket `session.start` configuration or WebRTC creation request:

```
{
  "store": true
}


```

Start the fork through the transport your application uses:

| Transport | Start the fork |
| --- | --- |
| WebSocket | Connect to `wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{source_session_id}/fork`. |
| WebRTC | Send a new SDP offer to `POST /v1/live/sessions/{source_session_id}/fork`. Apply the returned `transport.sdp` answer to the new peer connection. |

A fork inherits the source session’s model, original instructions, and input. Send only the supported overrides at startup:

- **WebSocket:**`store`, Responses delegation settings, and the new connection’s `audio.format`. Send a `session.start` event with a `session` object; use `{}` to keep inherited settings where supported.
- **WebRTC:**`store`, Responses delegation settings, and frontend client permissions.

For a WebSocket fork, set `audio.format` for the new connection or use the default PCM16 at 24 kHz. The source audio format and frontend data-channel permissions are not inherited. WebRTC negotiates audio format during connection setup; omit `audio.format`. WebRTC preserves frontend permission settings unless you override them.

For WebSocket, wait for `session.started` before sending more commands. For WebRTC, the HTTP request starts the session; continue through the negotiated connection without sending another `session.start`.

### Start a WebSocket fork

Set `OPENAI_API_KEY`. The examples use the stored source session ID saved by your application. They confirm startup and then close the fork. To continue the conversation, send and receive audio after `session.started` using the [WebSocket connection flow](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-websockets?api=live). See the [fork WebSocket reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/live/fork-websocket) for the startup fields and events.

TypeScript

```
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { ForksWS } from "openai/resources/live/forks/ws";

async function forkSession(sourceSessionId: string) {
  const ws = new ForksWS(new OpenAI(), { session_id: sourceSessionId });
  let finalized = false;
  let closeRequested = false;
  try {
    for await (const event of ws) {
      if (event.type === "open") {
        ws.send({ type: "session.start", session: {} });
      } else if (event.type === "error") {
        throw event.error;
      } else if (event.type === "message") {
        if (event.message.type === "session.started") {
          console.log("Fork ready:", event.message.session.id);
          // This startup example closes the fork after confirming it is ready.
          ws.send({ type: "session.close" });
          closeRequested = true;
        } else if (event.message.type === "session.closed") {
          console.log("Final usage:", event.message.usage);
          if (!closeRequested) {
            throw new Error("Fork ended before startup completed");
          }
          finalized = true;
          break;
        }
      }
    }
    if (!finalized) throw new Error("Connection closed before session.closed");
  } finally {
    ws.close();
  }
}
```

# Getting started with GPT-Live

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL.

GPT-Live handles a spoken conversation while a backend agent looks up information, uses tools, and completes tasks. It can listen while speaking (**full duplex**). Sending work to the backend is called **delegation**.

For example, a user can ask about an order and add a detail while the backend checks its status. GPT-Live can keep talking with the user and explain the result when it arrives. You choose the backend model or agent independently of the voice model.

## Understand the two parts

- **GPT-Live handles conversation.** It listens, speaks, and decides when to ask the backend for help. Give it a short prompt for conversation style and when to delegate.
- **The backend handles delegated tasks.** With Responses delegation, use a supported Responses model. With client delegation, connect any model, agent harness, or service your application runs. The backend reasons, uses tools, and returns results for GPT-Live to communicate. Keep detailed instructions, business rules, and tool workflows here.

Your application checks permissions, obtains required confirmations, runs functions that access your systems, and saves task progress. Backend work can continue when the caller interrupts the assistant; your application decides whether to finish or cancel it. See [Voice agents](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-agents) to compare GPT-Live with Realtime and chained voice applications.





## Choose how to run the backend

Start with **[Responses delegation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation?delegation-mode=responses#configure-responses-delegation)** to have OpenAI run the backend model and pass conversation context and results between it and GPT-Live. Your application still runs your own function tools. Choose **[client delegation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation?delegation-mode=client#configure-client-delegation)** to connect an existing agent or control the backend’s context, execution, and returned results yourself.

See [Choose a delegation mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#choose-a-delegation-mode) for the comparison and configuration details. Choose the mode when you create the session; to change modes, start a new session.

## Connect your first session

Start with the [GPT-Live WebRTC quickstart](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-webrtc?api=live). Its browser and server example connects microphone input and speaker output, with a Responses backend that can search the web.

You need a microphone, a browser page served over HTTPS or localhost, and a trusted server with an OpenAI project API key. Keep the key on the server.

1. Write a short [conversation prompt](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-prompting) that tells GPT-Live when to ask the backend for help.
2. Follow the quickstart to connect the browser's microphone, audio playback, and event channel. Your server creates the session and exchanges the browser's connection offer for an answer.
3. Wait for `session.started`, then speak and listen to a reply. Ask a question that needs current information to try the web search backend.
4. End the conversation and [close the session](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#usage-and-graceful-close) to collect final usage and release the connection.

For your first test, listen to the assistant and check that its answer reflects the backend’s search result.

GPT-Live voice sessions are billed by duration, per second. See the [model pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-live-1) for the current rate. Backend model and tool usage is billed separately. See [Cost optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-latency-cost?api=live) for usage accounting and ways to reduce costs.

## Sample apps and client SDKs

- **[OpenAI Live Console](https://github.com/openai/openai-live-console)** is a local sample app for exploring GPT-Live conversations, delegation, and backend tool activity.
- **[Switchboard OpenAI Live Toolkit](https://github.com/switchboard-sdk/openai-live-toolkit)** is a third-party React Native SDK for building GPT-Live applications on iOS.

## Choose a connection

- **[WebRTC](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-webrtc?api=live)** is recommended for audio connections in browser, mobile, and server applications. It carries audio on media tracks and JSON events on a data channel.
- **[WebSockets](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-websockets?api=live)** are a supported alternative. One connection carries audio and control events.
- **[Telephony and SIP](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-sip?api=live)** for connecting phone calls.

To monitor or control an existing session from your backend, add a [server-side connection](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-server-controls?api=live). This additional WebSocket is called a **sideband**; audio continues through the session’s primary connection.

## Partner integrations

If your application already uses **LiveKit**, **Twilio**, **Telnyx**, **Bandwidth**, or **Daily/Pipecat**, follow the [partner integration overview](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-partner-integrations) to connect its existing calls or audio streams to GPT-Live.

## Continue building

- Shape conversation style and delegation behavior in [Prompting GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-prompting).
- Connect tools and reduce backend latency in [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation).
- Manage context, transcripts, and session lifecycle in [Managing sessions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations).
- Choose a migration path for your Realtime or text-based agent in [Migrate to GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration).
- Test conversation and task outcomes in [Evaluating voice agents](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation).

# Migrate to GPT-Live

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL.

GPT-Live handles listening and speaking. A backend decides how to complete tasks and which tools to call. Keep your existing tool implementations, permission checks, and saved task records. During migration, connect that backend to GPT-Live and decide which instructions belong in each model.

This guide uses an appointment assistant: check availability, ask the user to confirm a slot, then book it. Start with a connected session from [Getting started](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live), and keep representative conversations from your existing application for comparison.

## Before you migrate

Record the requirements your migrated application must preserve:

- **Tools and business rules:** List your existing prompts, tools, and workflows, including the conditions for each action.
- **Input types:** Identify where audio, typed text, and images enter your application and which backend needs them. See [Add images and visual context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#add-images-and-visual-context).
- **Decisions that depend on audio:** Identify decisions that need the original sound, beyond the words in a transcript. See [Preserve decisions that depend on audio](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration?migration-path=realtime#preserve-decisions-that-depend-on-audio).
- **Speech and playback:** Specify when speech may start, when it must stop, and which checks must finish before audio plays.
- **Permissions and guardrails:** List authorization, confirmation, and input/output checks, and where your application enforces them. See [Adapt your guardrails](#adapt-your-guardrails).
- **Durable state:** Identify the records, task progress, and pending actions your application must keep across disconnects and new sessions.
- **Baseline conversations:** Save representative conversations and their starting state, expected tool actions, final application state, and spoken responses from your current application.

Use [Getting started](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live) for session setup and the [voice agent evaluation Cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation) to plan your comparison.

## Choose your delegation mode

Choose who will run the backend:

- **Responses delegation:** Configure a hosted Responses model to reason about tasks and select tools. Your application executes custom functions and returns their results. This is a useful starting point when your Realtime model currently selects those functions.
- **Client delegation:** Keep your existing agent or orchestrator. Your application supplies its conversation context, starts its work, and decides which results to send to GPT-Live.

Either mode can support either migration path. For example, a Realtime application with a separate backend agent can keep that agent through client delegation. See [Choose a delegation mode](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#choose-a-delegation-mode) for the full comparison.

## Choose your migration path

Start with [From Realtime API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration?migration-path=realtime#from-realtime-api) if your current voice model selects tools. Start with [From a text agent or chained pipeline](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration?migration-path=text-agent#from-a-text-agent-or-chained-pipeline) if you are keeping an existing agent and adding GPT-Live as its voice interface.



## From Realtime API

Start with the [GPT-Live prompting guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-prompting). Split your existing prompt between the voice model and the backend instead of copying it wholesale into `session.instructions`. Keep conversation style and delegation guidance in the voice prompt; move detailed workflows and tool-use instructions to the backend.

**Before:** the Realtime model handles speech and selects functions such as `check_availability` and `book_appointment`. Your application executes the functions and returns their results.

**After:** GPT-Live handles speech and delegates task work. The backend selects the same functions; your application still validates and executes them. The steps here use Responses delegation. If you retain an external agent, use the [client adapter](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration?migration-path=text-agent#connect-your-existing-agent) instead.

### How Responses delegation works

Configure the backend model, instructions, and tools in `delegation.responses`. When GPT-Live decides a request needs backend work, the Live service calls that Responses model and supplies relevant conversation context. The backend reasons about the task and selects tools. Your application still runs custom functions, enforces permissions, and returns their results.

For the appointment assistant:

1. The user asks which appointments are available on Friday, and GPT-Live delegates the request.
2. The Responses backend requests `check_availability`.
3. Your application runs the function, returns its result, and continues the backend response.
4. GPT-Live uses the answer from the backend to discuss available slots with the user.

GPT-Live can continue speaking while the backend works. Track the backend task and audio playback separately: use tool results to update task status and your player’s state to update the speaking indicator. See [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#configure-responses-delegation) for configuration and the full event flow.

### Adapt the connection and audio lifecycle

Replace Realtime session setup with the [GPT-Live connection procedure](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live). Recheck your transport's startup and audio format. WebRTC carries audio on media tracks and JSON events on the data channel. A primary WebSocket carries audio in JSON events.

If your Realtime application uses a server connection to monitor the call or enforce guardrails, adapt it to the [GPT-Live sideband connection](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-server-controls?api=live#attach-to-the-existing-session). Follow [Adapt your guardrails](#adapt-your-guardrails) for the changes to conversation checks and playback.

| Existing Realtime behavior                                                                            | GPT-Live adaptation                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Send WebSocket audio with `input_audio_buffer.append`.                                                | Send `session.input_audio.append`; its `audio` field contains base64 raw audio.                                 |
| Play `response.output_audio.delta` from its `delta` field.                                            | Play `session.output_audio.delta` from its `delta` field, in order.                                             |
| Commit audio or create a response to start a turn when using manual turn control.                     | Stream audio continuously. GPT-Live decides when to speak; remove manual audio commits and voice-turn triggers. |
| Track audio generation and response completion with `response.output_audio.done` and `response.done`. | GPT-Live has no corresponding event marking the end of each spoken response. Track playback in your client.     |
| Display user captions from input transcription events.                                                | Append `session.input_transcript.delta` text to the user's captions.                                            |
| Display assistant captions from `response.output_audio_transcript.delta`.                             | Append `session.output_transcript.delta` text to the assistant's captions.                                      |

**Generation and playback:** Drive the speaking indicator from your audio player. The server can finish generating while the player still has a second of audio queued. In Realtime, `response.output_audio.done` marks the end of generation and `response.done` ends the response stream; check `response.status` for interruption or failure. GPT-Live has no equivalent event for the end of each spoken response.

**Captions:** When input transcription is enabled, Realtime sends text fragments through `conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.delta` and a final transcript through `conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed`. In GPT-Live, append each fragment to the caller’s or assistant’s captions; both can change at once. Your application decides how to group text and tracks playback through the audio player. See [Display captions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#display-captions).

Use `response.create` to start or continue delegated Responses work. GPT-Live manages when to speak as it listens to the conversation. For startup, greetings, interruptions, and closing a session, follow [Managing sessions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations).

### Split conversation and backend instructions

When migrating a Realtime assistant to GPT-Live, start with your existing prompt. Move speaking style and turn-taking instructions into the Live prompt, and add rules for when to delegate. Keep task instructions and tool-use procedures in the backend prompt.

If you're adding voice to a text agent, [reuse its existing backend prompt](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#start-with-your-existing-backend-prompt) and write a Live prompt for the spoken interaction.

#### Keep the experience consistent

Keep your assistant’s role, audience, and purpose, and preserve the details that shape the conversation:

- Greetings, introductions, and spoken disclosures, including any required wording or order.
- Language and pronunciation requirements, such as “Speak English.”
- Personality, warmth, empathy, formality, and pacing.
- The level of detail in spoken answers and examples that show the intended style.
- How it acknowledges the user, pauses to listen, and responds to interruptions.

A short Live prompt can still ask for detailed spoken answers.

#### Write the Live prompt

Use the [recommended prompt structure](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-prompting#recommended-prompt-structure) for the assistant's identity, speaking style, and conversational behavior. Keep `Backchannel policy` and `Interruption policy` to describe listening acknowledgments and how the assistant responds when someone speaks over it.

Live needs to know what the backend can do so it can delegate accurately. Describe those capabilities in plain language. Function names and tool schemas belong in the backend, which handles tool calls.

Under `Delegation policy`, adapt these sections to your application:

- **`Backend tools`:** List the capabilities your application supports, using the same terms as your existing prompt. For example: “Check appointment availability and schedule callbacks.”
- **`Delegate to the backend when`:** State when to use those capabilities, such as “Delegate when the user asks to schedule a callback.” Include corrections, confirmations, and new details needed for work already in progress.
- **`Do not delegate to the backend when`:** Describe what Live can handle directly, such as a greeting, a brief clarification, or repeating information from the conversation or a still-current backend result.

Describe how Live should communicate progress, ask the backend's next question, or relay a verified result.

If your assistant ends calls, give Live instructions for the farewell and for delegating the end-call request. Put the actual end-call tool and sequence in the backend. For example, a procedure might require the application to finish playing the farewell, disconnect, cancel pending calculations, and block further saves. Live handles the farewell and delegation; the backend and application handle those remaining steps.

#### Adapt your backend prompt

Use your original prompt as the starting point. Keep its wording, order, examples, and structure wherever they still apply. If it mainly describes tasks, most of it can stay as written.

Keep instructions here for:

- Interpreting the user's request, applying corrections, collecting missing information, and tracking task progress.
- Using domain facts, checking eligibility, and consulting the records or services that establish the answer.
- Following procedures for searches, updates, confirmations, routing, transfers, callbacks, and other supported actions.
- Applying safety, privacy, and authorization rules, handling failures, and restricting actions after a transfer or call end.
- Preparing accurate facts, task status, and the next question for Live to communicate.

Move instructions for voice, greetings, turn-taking, and when to delegate into the Live prompt. Adapt instructions that assume the backend speaks directly to the user so it returns information for Live instead. Keep safety and privacy limits in both prompts wherever they affect what that model may say, ask, or do.

Keep function names, argument requirements, and tool-use procedures in backend instructions. Put tool definitions in your backend's tool configuration. Your application executes its tools and enforces permissions, argument validation, and required confirmations against the current task state.

Use the backend model to understand requests, corrections, and confirmations from the conversation. Regular expressions, keyword lists, and exact-phrase rules miss meaning that depends on earlier speech or a correction. For example, “yes” may confirm a slot, acknowledge a question, or refer to an earlier suggestion.

Preserve the rules for work already running when the caller interrupts or the call is transferred or ended. Stopping speech leaves backend work running. If the caller asks to cancel, the backend and application need to handle that cancellation and report its outcome to Live.

#### Resolve conflicting instructions

Review the original prompt and both new prompts for instructions that disagree. Combine repeated instructions, and keep specific conditions and exceptions alongside the rules they qualify. Check permissions, question limits, confirmations, and what may happen after a call ends.

Separate what the user wants from what has happened. If a caller changes Friday to Thursday, the latest request tells the backend to work on Thursday. The booking record tells it whether Friday was already booked. Your existing confirmation and authorization rules determine which changes it can make next.

Resolve product choices with the people responsible for them before using the prompts. For example, if one instruction says to continue a booking and another says to stop all work when the caller interrupts, decide which behavior the application should provide. Record the agreed behavior in the prompts and the application logic that enforces it.

Check that each required action has an implementation. Ending a call requires an end-call capability; a spoken goodbye alone leaves the connection open. If a capability is missing, decide whether to implement it or agree on a supported alternative with the team that owns the workflow.

#### Review both prompts

Compare both prompts with the original and check that every required behavior has a place:

- The Live prompt preserves the assistant's identity, vocabulary, speaking style, disclosures, and interruption behavior.
- The backend prompt preserves the task procedures, facts, conditions, examples, permissions, and failure handling.
- Delegation covers new requests, corrections, confirmations, and requests that combine conversation with task information.
- The two prompts agree on question limits, when an action is confirmed, and how to handle continuing work, cancellation, transfers, and call ending.

Put the Live prompt in `session.instructions`. For Responses delegation, put the backend prompt in `session.delegation.responses.instructions`; for client delegation, keep it in your existing agent's configuration. Keep tool definitions with the backend. See [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation) for configuration and result handling.

The function still returns a result for its original `call_id`. What changes is where your handler receives the call and sends the result:

| Continue after all required results. | Send `response.create`.                                                          | Send `response.create` to continue backend work.                                                                  |

Before booking, check that the date, slot, and confirmation still match the current request. If you decline a pending function call because the user changed the request, return a result that explains it was skipped or cancelled, matching what actually happened. Use that information to update the appropriate caller or assistant caption or chat bubble, including when a fragment arrives late or both people speak at once. # Prompting GPT-Live

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL.

`gpt-live-1` is a voice model for natural, continuous conversation. It can listen and speak at the same time, respond to interruptions, and keep the conversation moving while a backend agent handles reasoning, tools, and longer tasks.

Use `session.instructions` for the assistant’s role, speaking style, and when to ask the backend for help. Give the backend model or agent the procedures and tools for tasks such as looking up an order or changing a booking.

Describe the conversational behavior you want, and let GPT-Live choose the wording for ordinary replies. When migrating from Realtime, keep the rules your product needs for wording, interruptions, and the order of actions. Test the simpler prompt on representative conversations as you revise it.

Your application checks permissions and required confirmations before executing an action.

To adapt an existing Realtime prompt, follow [Split conversation and backend instructions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration?migration-path=realtime#split-conversation-and-backend-instructions).

## Recommended prompt structure

Start with this template and add instructions as needed. See [session configuration](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#configuration-fields) for field limits.

Keep the template’s `Backchannel policy`, `Interruption policy`, and `Delegation policy` headings, and customize the text beneath them. Backchannels are brief listening sounds, such as “mm-hmm,” that the assistant can make while the caller continues speaking.

For `gpt-live-1`, use the instruction `Generate <|SpawnThinking|>` when the model should request backend work, rather than “delegate to the backend.”

```text
You are [name], a calm, friendly voice assistant for [service].
Speak warmly and naturally, at an unhurried pace. Be clear and direct, not overly cheerful.
If the user is frustrated, acknowledge it briefly and focus on the next helpful step.

Backchannel policy: Use moderate backchannels. Acknowledge naturally without competing with the main response.

Interruption policy: Stop speaking when the user interrupts. Listen to what they say.

Delegation policy:
Backend tools:
- [capability]: [what the backend can do]

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The request needs a backend capability or careful reasoning.
- A correction changes the work already requested.

Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- You can answer from the conversation or a still-current result.
- You need a brief clarification to understand the request.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work.
Do not guess the result while waiting.
```

List the capabilities your backend supports. GPT-Live uses this list to decide which requests to hand off. Configure the backend’s actual tools in [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation).

## Delegation

In the `Delegation policy` section, list the backend’s capabilities and the requests that should trigger a handoff. Use concrete conditions, such as “the user asks to change a booking.” Keep the template’s three labels: `Backend tools`, `Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when`, and `Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when`.

For a booking assistant, replace the starter template’s entire delegation section with:

```text
Delegation policy:
Backend tools:
- Appointments: check available times and create, change, or cancel bookings.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The user asks for availability or wants to create, change, or cancel a booking.
- A correction changes a booking task already in progress.
- The answer needs careful reasoning beyond a simple reply.

Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The user greets you or asks you to repeat a result already provided.
- You cannot tell what they are asking for without a brief clarification.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work.
Do not guess the result while waiting.
```

Test the policy with requests that need backend work, conversational replies the voice model can handle, and corrections to work already in progress.

A spoken promise such as “I’m checking that” does not confirm that backend work has started. The prompt should request delegation through `<|SpawnThinking|>`.

Put the full task procedure in the backend instructions and define tools in the backend’s tool configuration. Have GPT-Live wait for the backend’s result before stating a price, confirming a booking, or reporting that an action is complete.

You can prompt GPT-Live to acknowledge a request while delegated work runs. As background work progresses, use [`session.commentary.append`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#keep-updates-accurate-and-useful) to provide updates you want GPT-Live to say aloud.

For backend prompts, conversation context, tool results, typed input, and API examples, read [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation). For the architecture overview, read [Getting started with GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live).

## Personality

GPT-Live is steerable but requires thoughtful prompting. Choose or create a voice, then use system instructions to shape its personality and behavior:

1. **Choose the voice itself.** Use a built-in voice, a [custom voice created from a recording](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/custom-voices#create-a-voice-from-a-recording), or use [prompt-to-voice](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/custom-voices#create-a-voice-from-a-description) to design a voice from a description.
2. **Shape its personality and behavior.** Describe its character, patience, and response to interruptions. You can also guide delivery, such as a whisper or an animated explanation.

**Describe sound and behavior separately.** For a tutor, specify both the vocal qualities and how it should teach: for example, give one hint, then give the learner time to think.

**Audition the actual combination of voice and instructions.** Try it in conversations your application will use.

Recipes show the **voice choice** and **personality prompt**, which guides how the assistant speaks and behaves. For voices created with prompt-to-voice, they also show the **voice design prompt**, which describes the sound of the voice, and **voice design sample text**, the text supplied when creating that voice. You can describe the voice in a different language from the desired output, but use sample text in the `script_hint` in the language you want the voice to speak. For a bilingual voice, include both languages in `script_hint` and describe how the voice should sound in each language. The [recipe download](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/personality-recipes.json) includes the complete recording inputs. The recordings use AI-generated voices and callers. Exact wording and behavior can vary when you try a prompt.

These excerpts cover personality and delivery. Keep your application's task,
  tool, and delegation instructions alongside them.

### Backchannels

Backchannels are brief listening sounds, such as “mm-hm,” while the user is speaking. Use a backchannel policy to describe how often you want them. Tune these separately from acknowledgments such as “Got it” at the start of an answer or tool call. If you want backchannels, allow brief listening sounds during interruptions; a rule that forbids all overlapping speech can suppress them.

You can vary both the content and frequency of backchannels. Try these policies to modify frequency.

<details>
<summary>None</summary>

```text
Backchannel policy: Do not produce any backchannel interjections while the user is speaking. Backchanneling is entirely disallowed—stay silent until it is your turn to respond.
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Frequent</summary>

```text
Backchannel policy: Use frequent short backchannels to signal active listening while keeping answers clear.
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Very frequent</summary>

```text
Backchannel policy: Use very frequent, varied backchannels for lively spoken rhythm. Keep each one brief and non-repetitive.
```

</details>



#### Relaxed whiteboarding

Voice: Stone · Standard voice

[Listen to Relaxed whiteboarding](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/jules-relaxed-whiteboarding-take2-eb70b3fad393.flac)

**Personality prompt**

```text
You are Jules, an easygoing voice partner for brainstorming at a whiteboard. Speak casually, with contractions, a relaxed, musing cadence, and little thinking pauses; offer one unexpected possibility in two short sentences, then leave room for the user. If the user feels stuck, lower the pressure and play with a rough idea together; explore possibilities without grading their performance. Backchannel policy: Backchannel frequently while the user thinks aloud: brief, varied “mm-hmm,” “yeah,” “oh,” or a warm little laugh after most completed thoughts. Keep listening; save ideas until invited. Interruption policy: Yield immediately to a new idea, correction, or “wait.” A brief “mm-hmm” from the user means keep going, not a new turn. Follow their changed direction.
```

#### Encouraging coach

Voice: Stone · Standard voice

[Listen to Encouraging coach](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/backchannel-stone-encouraging-coach-806a5b76beae.flac)

**Personality prompt**

```text
You are an encouraging coach listening to someone reflect on a challenging workout. Sound warm, energized and grounded, with a smile and forward-moving rhythm. Use compact, buoyant listening cues such as 'yeah,' 'mm-hmm,' 'there you go,' and 'that's it.' React with extra warmth when they notice their own improvement. Keep the encouragement conversational and brief, never shouted or a motivational speech.

Backchannel policy: Give lots of frequent, varied, audible little listening cues DURING the caller's turn, starting early and continuing as the story unfolds. Aim for roughly eight to twelve small reactions over half a minute; this is intent, not a count to say aloud. Keep each cue short, usually under a second. Brief overlap is welcome. Leave enough space and keep the cues light enough that the caller's words remain intelligible. Do not save all your reactions for the final answer.

Interruption policy: The caller keeps the floor through your cues and short thinking pauses. Listening sounds are welcome while the caller is speaking; questions, corrections, advice and full answers wait for the explicit invitation at the end. Then give one brief natural sentence that responds to what they said, and stop. If the caller resumes speaking during an answer, yield the substantive answer and keep listening.
```

I can explain the steps, listen to your ideas, or leave a little room for you to think. Whatever we choose, we will finish one thing before moving on to the next. That usually makes the whole process easier to follow.
```

**Personality prompt**

```text
Speak very slowly and deliberately, at about half your usual speaking speed. Lengthen the spoken syllables themselves while keeping the voice natural. Use only brief sentence pauses; do not achieve the slower pace by inserting long silences. Keep this unhurried articulation steady through the final sentence.
```



### Interruptions

GPT-Live is full duplex and can speak at the same time as the user. Instructions can encourage it to yield when interrupted, but they do not provide precise control over when it stops speaking. The model may keep speaking briefly after an interruption. Test both short interjections, such as “stop” or “wait,” and longer requests with your selected voice.



#### Immediate stop · Marin

Voice: Marin · Standard voice

[Listen to Immediate stop · Marin](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/interruption-marin-immediate-r2-b-marin-4bbe6b7f532f.flac#t=12.635708333333334)

**Personality prompt**

```text
Interruption policy: When the user interrupts, stop speaking right away, even in the middle of a sentence. Listen until they finish, then respond to what they said.

A brief acknowledgment like “sure” is okay when you stop speaking. Then listen until the user finishes; don't continue your explanation or answer early.
If the user asks you to stop or wait, corrects an important detail, describes an urgent problem, or asks to end the conversation, stop right away, without finishing your sentence or adding an acknowledgment.
Respond to the user's latest request. Don't resume an answer they've replaced.
```



Handle changes to a task separately from interruptions to speech. “Stop talking” asks the assistant to yield; “Cancel my booking” asks the backend to take an action. Have the backend process a changed or canceled request and return the outcome for the assistant to explain. Stopping speech leaves backend work running. If the user changes the task, update the application's active work too.

### Patience

Give a tutor room to wait through pauses and offer hints. Ask a debater for a quick challenge and a short follow-up. Both should yield when asked to pause. Patience is about when to respond, not just speaking slowly.

The bilingual Hindi tutor gives an English-speaking learner time to try a phrase. The Borough debate partner is prompted to jump in with objections. These are different voices and tasks, rather than two levels of a single control.

Set when the assistant may interrupt separately from how it should yield when the user interrupts. For selective interjections, you can try this instruction:

```text
Interrupt only when it materially improves the exchange, such as preventing a major misunderstanding or keeping the task on track.
```

Preserve the natural Indian English vowel shapes and rhythm when speaking English; pronounce Hindi naturally with clear dental and retroflex distinctions. Sound like a real adult in a one-to-one conversation, not a television announcer or a comic accent.
```

Good, let us work on just the first sound. We will keep the explanation in English and practise the Hindi together. Learning a language takes a little practice every day. You do not have to get every sound right on the first attempt. Listen carefully, notice where your tongue goes, and try again when you are ready. नमस्ते। मेरा नाम अनिका है। आप कैसे हैं? मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। We can break a long phrase into two smaller pieces. First say the beginning, then add the ending. Keep your voice relaxed. It is all right to laugh, make a mistake, and start again. We are having a conversation, not taking an exam.
```
