Keep the instruction application-authored. Do not copy untrusted user text into it as an instruction. Use `delegation_id: null` for this session-wide correction, and keep `content` within 500 tokens.

Match `session.instructions.appended` to your command through `client_event_id`. The acknowledgment arrives after estimated context injection. To stop audio reaching the caller, use the playback controls below.

For disclosures that request specific spoken wording, also use instructions. See [Deliver a disclosure](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#deliver-a-disclosure) for an example and playback considerations.

### Control playback when needed

If your application needs to block model audio, control playback at the client or media relay. Temporarily mute or drop the output, discard locally queued audio, and send the corrective instruction. Resume playback according to your application's recovery policy after clearing stale audio; an instruction acknowledgment is not a signal to resume. A sideband alone does not control playback, and corrective instructions cannot retract audio the caller has already heard.

`session.input_audio.mute` controls the caller's microphone input. It does not mute model output or cancel delegated work.

### Check speech before playback

For most applications, [monitor user and assistant transcripts](#run-checks-alongside-the-conversation) while the conversation continues. When a guardrail triggers, your application can block affected actions or send corrective instructions.

If your application needs to check assistant speech before playback, buffer the audio in your player or media bridge before sending it to the caller. Keep receiving audio and transcript events while the check runs, and read transcripts independently of playback.

1. **Collect audio and its transcript.** Implement output voice activity detection (VAD) in your application, or use a noise gate provided by your media framework, to identify candidate speech segments. GPT-Live does not provide an output VAD or noise gate for this workflow. Wait for the transcript needed to check each segment.
2. **Release approved audio.** When a segment passes the check, enqueue its original buffered audio for playback. If the check fails, the transcript is missing, or the check times out, discard the segment and use an application-defined safe fallback.
3. **Handle interruptions.** Associate the audio, transcript, check result, and playback state with an application-generated ID. When an interruption cancels that speech, clear its buffered and queued audio and ignore any later approval for it.

A pause can mark a candidate segment while the model is still composing an answer. If your policy requires checking a complete answer, define how your application establishes completion; voice activity detection alone cannot establish that the whole answer is finished.

Buffering adds latency. Discarded speech remains in the model’s conversation context, so test how the conversation continues after withheld audio or a fallback.

### Test the intervention

Test allowed and blocked requests, false positives, slow or failed checks, a trigger during speech, a trigger while a tool is running, and late results from canceled work. Verify action blocking, application state, corrective speech, and actual playback separately. If you control output, include queued audio and recovery in the test. Use the [voice agent evaluation Cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation) to compare task success and spoken response time.

## Finish cleanly

Keep receiving events while tools finish and the session reports final usage. Register the `session.closed` handler before sending `session.close`, and keep the WebRTC connection, data channel, and sideband open while pending work drains. Save the final session usage and any backend usage received in Responses events before cleanup. If the connection fails before the final event arrives, record finalization as incomplete. See [Managing sessions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#usage-and-graceful-close) for the close sequence.

  

  


The Realtime API allows clients to connect directly to the API server via WebRTC or SIP. However, you'll most likely want tool use and other business logic to reside on your application server to keep this logic private and client-agnostic.

Keep tool use, business logic, and other details secure on the server side by connecting over a “sideband” control channel. We now have sideband options for both SIP and WebRTC connections.

A sideband connection means there are two active connections to the same Realtime session: one from the user's client and one from your application server. The server connection can be used to monitor the session, update instructions, and respond to tool calls.

## With WebRTC

1. When [establishing a peer connection](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-webrtc?api=realtime) you fetch and receive an SDP response from the Realtime API to configure the connection. If you used the sample code from the WebRTC guide, that looks something like this:

```typescript
const baseUrl = "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls";
const sdpResponse = await fetch(baseUrl, {
  method: "POST",
  body: offer.sdp,
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${EPHEMERAL_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/sdp",
  },
});
```


2. The fetch response will contain a `Location` header that has a unique call ID that can be used on the server to establish a WebSocket connection to that same Realtime session.

```typescript
// Location: /v1/realtime/calls/rtc_123456
const location = sdpResponse.headers.get("Location");
const callId = location?.split("/").pop();
console.log(callId);
```


3. On a server, you can then [listen for events and configure the session](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations) just as you would from a typical Realtime API WebSocket connection, using that call ID with the URL
   `wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=rtc_xxxxx`, as shown below:

```typescript
import WebSocket from "ws";
const callId = "rtc_u1_9c6574da8b8a41a18da9308f4ad974ce";

// Connect to a WebSocket for the in-progress call
const url = "wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=" + callId;
const ws = new WebSocket(url, {
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer " + process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY,
  },
});

ws.on("open", function open() {
  console.log("Connected to server.");

  // Send client events over the WebSocket once connected
  ws.send(
    JSON.stringify({
      type: "session.update",
      session: {
        type: "realtime",
        instructions: "Be extra nice today!",
      },
    })
  );
});

// Listen for and parse server events
ws.on("message", function incoming(message) {
  console.log(JSON.parse(message.toString()));
});
```


In Go, pass the call ID to your server-side session update function:

```go
func updateSession(ctx context.Context, client openai.Client, callID string) error {
	conn, err := client.Realtime.Connect(ctx, realtime.RealtimeConnectionOptions{}, option.WithQuery("call_id", callID))
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer conn.Close()
	if err := conn.Send(ctx, realtime.RealtimeClientEventParamOfSessionUpdate(realtime.RealtimeSessionCreateRequestParam{
		Instructions: openai.String("Be extra nice today!"),
	})); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	for {
		event, err := conn.Recv(ctx)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if event.Type == "error" {
			return fmt.Errorf("Realtime API error: %s", event.OfRealtimeErrorEvent.Error.Message)
		}
		if event.Type == "session.updated" {
			if event.OfSessionUpdatedEvent.Session.OfRealtimeSessionCreateRequest.Instructions != "Be extra nice today!" {
				return fmt.Errorf("session update was not applied")
			}
			fmt.Println("session.updated")
			return nil
		}
	}
}
```

```ruby
require "openai"

# Use the call ID from the WebRTC creation Location header or SIP webhook.
call_id = ENV.fetch("OPENAI_CALL_ID")
client = OpenAI::Client.new
client.realtime.connect_to_call(call_id: call_id) do |connection|
  connection.session.update(type: :realtime, instructions: "Be extra nice today!")
  updated = connection.find do |event|
    raise event.error.message if event.is_a?(OpenAI::Realtime::RealtimeErrorEvent)

    if event.is_a?(OpenAI::Realtime::SessionUpdatedEvent)
      session = event.session
      raise "Session update was not applied" unless session.is_a?(OpenAI::Realtime::RealtimeSessionCreateRequest) && session.instructions == "Be extra nice today!"

      puts "session.updated"
      true
    else
      false
    end
  end
  raise "Connection closed before the session update" unless updated
end
```


In this way, you are able to add tools, monitor sessions, and carry out business logic on the server instead of needing to configure those actions on the client.

## With SIP

1. A user connects to OpenAI via phone over SIP.
2. OpenAI sends a webhook to your application’s server webhook URL, notifying your app of the state of the session. The webhook will look something like:

```json
POST https://my_website.com/webhook_endpoint
user-agent: OpenAI/1.0 (+https://platform.openai.com/docs/webhooks)
content-type: application/json
webhook-id: wh_685342e6c53c8190a1be43f081506c52 # unique id for idempotency
webhook-timestamp: 1750287078 # timestamp of delivery attempt
webhook-signature: v1,REDACTED # signature to verify authenticity from OpenAI

{
  "object": "event",
  "id": "evt_685343a1381c819085d44c354e1b330e",
  "type": "realtime.call.incoming",
  "created_at": 1750287018, // Unix timestamp
  "data": {
    "call_id": "some_unique_id",
    "sip_headers": [
      { "name": "From", "value": "sip:+142555512112@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "To", "value": "sip:+18005551212@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "Call-ID", "value": "03782086-4ce9-44bf-8b0d-4e303d2cc590"}
    ]
  }
}

```

3. The application server opens a WebSocket connection to the Realtime API using the `call_id` value provided in the webhook, via a URL like this: `wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id={callId}`. The WebSocket connection will live for the life of the SIP call.

The WebSocket connection can then be used to send and receive events to control the call, just as you would if the session was initiated with a WebSocket connection. This includes monitoring the call, updating instructions dynamically, and responding to tool calls.

# Prompting GPT-Live

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL.

`gpt-live-1` is a voice model for natural, continuous conversation. It can listen and speak at the same time, respond to interruptions, and keep the conversation moving while a backend agent handles reasoning, tools, and longer tasks.

Use `session.instructions` for the assistant’s role, speaking style, and when to ask the backend for help. Give the backend model or agent the procedures and tools for tasks such as looking up an order or changing a booking.

Describe the conversational behavior you want, and let GPT-Live choose the wording for ordinary replies. When migrating from Realtime, keep the rules your product needs for wording, interruptions, and the order of actions. Test the simpler prompt on representative conversations as you revise it.

Your application checks permissions and required confirmations before executing an action.

To adapt an existing Realtime prompt, follow [Split conversation and backend instructions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-migration?migration-path=realtime#split-conversation-and-backend-instructions).

## Recommended prompt structure

Start with this template and add instructions as needed. See [session configuration](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#configuration-fields) for field limits.

Keep the template’s `Backchannel policy`, `Interruption policy`, and `Delegation policy` headings, and customize the text beneath them. Backchannels are brief listening sounds, such as “mm-hmm,” that the assistant can make while the caller continues speaking.

For `gpt-live-1`, use the instruction `Generate <|SpawnThinking|>` when the model should request backend work, rather than “delegate to the backend.”

```text
You are [name], a calm, friendly voice assistant for [service].
Speak warmly and naturally, at an unhurried pace. Be clear and direct, not overly cheerful.
If the user is frustrated, acknowledge it briefly and focus on the next helpful step.

Backchannel policy: Use moderate backchannels. Acknowledge naturally without competing with the main response.

Interruption policy: Stop speaking when the user interrupts. Listen to what they say.

Delegation policy:
Backend tools:
- [capability]: [what the backend can do]

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The request needs a backend capability or careful reasoning.
- A correction changes the work already requested.

Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- You can answer from the conversation or a still-current result.
- You need a brief clarification to understand the request.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work.
Do not guess the result while waiting.
```

List the capabilities your backend supports. GPT-Live uses this list to decide which requests to hand off. Configure the backend’s actual tools in [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation).

## Delegation

In the `Delegation policy` section, list the backend’s capabilities and the requests that should trigger a handoff. Use concrete conditions, such as “the user asks to change a booking.” Keep the template’s three labels: `Backend tools`, `Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when`, and `Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when`.

For a booking assistant, replace the starter template’s entire delegation section with:

```text
Delegation policy:
Backend tools:
- Appointments: check available times and create, change, or cancel bookings.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The user asks for availability or wants to create, change, or cancel a booking.
- A correction changes a booking task already in progress.
- The answer needs careful reasoning beyond a simple reply.

Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The user greets you or asks you to repeat a result already provided.
- You cannot tell what they are asking for without a brief clarification.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work.
Do not guess the result while waiting.
```

Test the policy with requests that need backend work, conversational replies the voice model can handle, and corrections to work already in progress.

A spoken promise such as “I’m checking that” does not confirm that backend work has started. The prompt should request delegation through `<|SpawnThinking|>`.

Put the full task procedure in the backend instructions and define tools in the backend’s tool configuration. Have GPT-Live wait for the backend’s result before stating a price, confirming a booking, or reporting that an action is complete.

You can prompt GPT-Live to acknowledge a request while delegated work runs. As background work progresses, use [`session.commentary.append`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#keep-updates-accurate-and-useful) to provide updates you want GPT-Live to say aloud.

For backend prompts, conversation context, tool results, typed input, and API examples, read [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation). For the architecture overview, read [Getting started with GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live).

## Personality

GPT-Live is steerable but requires thoughtful prompting. Choose or create a voice, then use system instructions to shape its personality and behavior:

1. **Choose the voice itself.** Use a built-in voice, a [custom voice created from a recording](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/custom-voices#create-a-voice-from-a-recording), or use [prompt-to-voice](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/custom-voices#create-a-voice-from-a-description) to design a voice from a description.
2. **Shape its personality and behavior.** Describe its character, patience, and response to interruptions. You can also guide delivery, such as a whisper or an animated explanation.

**Describe sound and behavior separately.** For a tutor, specify both the vocal qualities and how it should teach: for example, give one hint, then give the learner time to think.

**Audition the actual combination of voice and instructions.** Try it in conversations your application will use.

Recipes show the **voice choice** and **personality prompt**, which guides how the assistant speaks and behaves. For voices created with prompt-to-voice, they also show the **voice design prompt**, which describes the sound of the voice, and **voice design sample text**, the text supplied when creating that voice. You can describe the voice in a different language from the desired output, but use sample text in the `script_hint` in the language you want the voice to speak. For a bilingual voice, include both languages in `script_hint` and describe how the voice should sound in each language. The [recipe download](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/personality-recipes.json) includes the complete recording inputs. The recordings use AI-generated voices and callers. Exact wording and behavior can vary when you try a prompt.

These excerpts cover personality and delivery. Keep your application's task,
  tool, and delegation instructions alongside them.

### Backchannels

Backchannels are brief listening sounds, such as “mm-hm,” while the user is speaking. Use a backchannel policy to describe how often you want them. Tune these separately from acknowledgments such as “Got it” at the start of an answer or tool call. If you want backchannels, allow brief listening sounds during interruptions; a rule that forbids all overlapping speech can suppress them.

You can vary both the content and frequency of backchannels. Try these policies to modify frequency.

<details>
<summary>None</summary>

```text
Backchannel policy: Do not produce any backchannel interjections while the user is speaking. Backchanneling is entirely disallowed—stay silent until it is your turn to respond.
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Frequent</summary>

```text
Backchannel policy: Use frequent short backchannels to signal active listening while keeping answers clear.
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Very frequent</summary>

```text
Backchannel policy: Use very frequent, varied backchannels for lively spoken rhythm. Keep each one brief and non-repetitive.
```

</details>



#### Relaxed whiteboarding

Voice: Stone · Standard voice

[Listen to Relaxed whiteboarding](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/jules-relaxed-whiteboarding-take2-eb70b3fad393.flac)

**Personality prompt**

```text
You are Jules, an easygoing voice partner for brainstorming at a whiteboard. Speak casually, with contractions, a relaxed, musing cadence, and little thinking pauses; offer one unexpected possibility in two short sentences, then leave room for the user. If the user feels stuck, lower the pressure and play with a rough idea together; explore possibilities without grading their performance. Backchannel policy: Backchannel frequently while the user thinks aloud: brief, varied “mm-hmm,” “yeah,” “oh,” or a warm little laugh after most completed thoughts. Keep listening; save ideas until invited. Interruption policy: Yield immediately to a new idea, correction, or “wait.” A brief “mm-hmm” from the user means keep going, not a new turn. Follow their changed direction.
```

#### Encouraging coach

Voice: Stone · Standard voice

[Listen to Encouraging coach](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/backchannel-stone-encouraging-coach-806a5b76beae.flac)

**Personality prompt**

```text
You are an encouraging coach listening to someone reflect on a challenging workout. Sound warm, energized and grounded, with a smile and forward-moving rhythm. Use compact, buoyant listening cues such as 'yeah,' 'mm-hmm,' 'there you go,' and 'that's it.' React with extra warmth when they notice their own improvement. Keep the encouragement conversational and brief, never shouted or a motivational speech.

Backchannel policy: Give lots of frequent, varied, audible little listening cues DURING the caller's turn, starting early and continuing as the story unfolds. Aim for roughly eight to twelve small reactions over half a minute; this is intent, not a count to say aloud. Keep each cue short, usually under a second. Brief overlap is welcome. Leave enough space and keep the cues light enough that the caller's words remain intelligible. Do not save all your reactions for the final answer.

Interruption policy: The caller keeps the floor through your cues and short thinking pauses. Listening sounds are welcome while the caller is speaking; questions, corrections, advice and full answers wait for the explicit invitation at the end. Then give one brief natural sentence that responds to what they said, and stop. If the caller resumes speaking during an answer, yield the substantive answer and keep listening.
```

```text
Speak very slowly and deliberately, at about half your usual speaking speed. Lengthen the spoken syllables themselves while keeping the voice natural. Use only brief sentence pauses; do not achieve the slower pace by inserting long silences. Keep this unhurried articulation steady through the final sentence.
```



### Interruptions

GPT-Live is full duplex and can speak at the same time as the user. Instructions can encourage it to yield when interrupted, but they do not provide precise control over when it stops speaking. The model may keep speaking briefly after an interruption. Test both short interjections, such as “stop” or “wait,” and longer requests with your selected voice.



#### Immediate stop · Marin

Voice: Marin · Standard voice

[Listen to Immediate stop · Marin](https://developers.openai.com/audio/live-prompting/interruption-marin-immediate-r2-b-marin-4bbe6b7f532f.flac#t=12.635708333333334)

**Personality prompt**

```text
Interruption policy: When the user interrupts, stop speaking right away, even in the middle of a sentence. Listen until they finish, then respond to what they said.

A brief acknowledgment like “sure” is okay when you stop speaking. Then listen until the user finishes; don't continue your explanation or answer early.
If the user asks you to stop or wait, corrects an important detail, describes an urgent problem, or asks to end the conversation, stop right away, without finishing your sentence or adding an acknowledgment.
Respond to the user's latest request. Don't resume an answer they've replaced.
```



Handle changes to a task separately from interruptions to speech. “Stop talking” asks the assistant to yield; “Cancel my booking” asks the backend to take an action. Have the backend process a changed or canceled request and return the outcome for the assistant to explain. Stopping speech leaves backend work running. If the user changes the task, update the application's active work too.

### Patience

Give a tutor room to wait through pauses and offer hints. Ask a debater for a quick challenge and a short follow-up. Both should yield when asked to pause. Patience is about when to respond, not just speaking slowly.

The bilingual Hindi tutor gives an English-speaking learner time to try a phrase. The Borough debate partner is prompted to jump in with objections. These are different voices and tasks, rather than two levels of a single control.

Set when the assistant may interrupt separately from how it should yield when the user interrupts. For selective interjections, you can try this instruction:

```text
Interrupt only when it materially improves the exchange, such as preventing a major misunderstanding or keeping the task on track.
```

The recordings below use their own personality prompts, shown on each card.

Voice: Custom generated with prompt-to-voice

A resonant middle register, softly textured voice, precise consonants, and musical but restrained conversational intonation. Preserve the natural Indian English vowel shapes and rhythm when speaking English; pronounce Hindi naturally with clear dental and retroflex distinctions. Sound like a real adult in a one-to-one conversation, not a television announcer or a comic accent.

Your application configures and runs the backend: choose its model or service, instructions, tools, and routing. If the backend uses the Responses API, set its model and tools in your application's Responses requests.

When GPT-Live requests help, build the backend request from your saved conversation history and current task state. Check permissions and required confirmations, run the work, and choose which results to return.

## Keep the conversation context in your application

For client delegation, **collect transcripts and keep the current task state yourself**.

Listen for `session.input_transcript.delta` and `session.output_transcript.delta`. These events contain transcript text in `delta`, along with `start_ms` and `end_ms` timestamps. Keep enough history to understand short replies such as “yes,” corrections such as “Thursday, not Friday,” and details supplied earlier. A transcript fragment is not a complete user turn, and transcripts may contain mistakes.

The separate `session.delegation.created` event contains an `offset_ms` timestamp and delegation metadata, including `delegation.id` and `delegation.target`. It does **not** contain the user's utterance or task text. Use the transcript events and application state to work out what the user wants. Save `delegation.id` so you can match updates to that request.

Keep long records and full tool output in the backend. If you create a replacement session, restore the relevant context from your application and check which actions already ran before repeating any work.

## Control playback when needed

If your application needs to block model audio, control playback at the client or media relay. Temporarily mute or drop the output, discard locally queued audio, and send the corrective instruction. Resume playback according to your application's recovery policy after clearing stale audio; an instruction acknowledgment is not a signal to resume. A sideband alone does not control playback, and corrective instructions cannot retract audio the caller has already heard.

`session.input_audio.mute` controls the caller's microphone input. It does not mute model output or cancel delegated work.

### Check speech before playback

For most applications, [monitor user and assistant transcripts](#run-checks-alongside-the-conversation) while the conversation continues. When a guardrail triggers, your application can block affected actions or send corrective instructions.

If your application needs to check assistant speech before playback, buffer the audio in your player or media bridge before sending it to the caller. Keep receiving audio and transcript events while the check runs, and read transcripts independently of playback.

1. **Collect audio and its transcript.** Implement output voice activity detection (VAD) in your application, or use a noise gate provided by your media framework, to identify candidate speech segments. GPT-Live does not provide an output VAD or noise gate for this workflow. Wait for the transcript needed to check each segment.
2. **Release approved audio.** When a segment passes the check, enqueue its original buffered audio for playback. If the check fails, the transcript is missing, or the check times out, discard the segment and use an application-defined safe fallback.
3. **Handle interruptions.** Associate the audio, transcript, check result, and playback state with an application-generated ID. When an interruption cancels that speech, clear its buffered and queued audio and ignore any later approval for it.

A pause can mark a candidate segment while the model is still composing an answer. If your policy requires checking a complete answer, define how your application establishes completion; voice activity detection alone cannot establish that the whole answer is finished.

Buffering adds latency. Discarded speech remains in the model’s conversation context, so test how the conversation continues after withheld audio or a fallback.

### Test the intervention

Test allowed and blocked requests, false positives, slow or failed checks, a trigger during speech, a trigger while a tool is running, and late results from canceled work. Verify action blocking, application state, corrective speech, and actual playback separately. If you control output, include queued audio and recovery in the test. Use the [voice agent evaluation Cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/audio/voice_agent_evaluation) to compare task success and spoken response time.

## Finish cleanly

Keep receiving events while tools finish and the session reports final usage. Register the `session.closed` handler before sending `session.close`, and keep the WebRTC connection, data channel, and sideband open while pending work drains. Save the final session usage and any backend usage received in Responses events before cleanup. If the connection fails before the final event arrives, record finalization as incomplete. See [Managing sessions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#us

## Recommended prompt structure

Start with this template and add instructions as needed. See [session configuration](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#configuration-fields) for field limits.

Keep the template’s `Backchannel policy`, `Interruption policy`, and `Delegation policy` headings, and customize the text beneath them. Backchannels are brief listening sounds, such as “mm-hmm,” that the assistant can make while the caller continues speaking.

For `gpt-live-1`, use the instruction `Generate <|SpawnThinking|>` when the model should request backend work, rather than “delegate to the backend.”

```text
You are [name], a calm, friendly voice assistant for [service].
Speak warmly and naturally, at an unhurried pace. Be clear and direct, not overly cheerful.
If the user is frustrated, acknowledge it briefly and focus on the next helpful step.

Backchannel policy: Use moderate backchannels. Acknowledge naturally without competing with the main response.

Interruption policy: Stop speaking when the user interrupts. Listen to what they say.

Delegation policy:
Backend tools:
- [capability]: [what the backend can do]

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The request needs a backend capability or careful reasoning.
- A correction changes the work already requested.

Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- You can answer from the conversation or a still-current result.
- You need a brief clarification to understand the request.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work.
Do not guess the result while waiting.
```

List the capabilities your backend supports. GPT-Live uses this list to decide which requests to hand off. Configure the backend’s actual tools in [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation).

## Delegation

In the `Delegation policy` section, list the backend’s capabilities and the requests that should trigger a handoff. Use concrete conditions, such as “the user asks to change a booking.” Keep the template’s three labels: `Backend tools`, `Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when`, and `Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when`.

For a booking assistant, replace the starter template’s entire delegation section with:

```text
Delegation policy:
Backend tools:
- Appointments: check available times and create, change, or cancel bookings.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The user asks for availability or wants to create, change, or cancel a booking.
- A correction changes a booking task already in progress.
- The answer needs careful reasoning beyond a simple reply.

Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when:
- The user greets you or asks you to repeat a result already provided.
- You cannot tell what they are asking for without a brief clarification.

Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work.
Do not guess the result while waiting.
```

Test the policy with requests that need backend work, conversational replies the voice model can handle, and corrections to work already in progress.

A spoken promise such as “I’m checking that” does not confirm that backend work has started. The prompt should request delegation through `<|SpawnThinking|>`.

Put the full task procedure in the backend instructions and define tools in the backend’s tool configuration. Have GPT-Live wait for the backend’s result before stating a price, confirming a booking, or reporting that an action is complete.

You can prompt GPT-Live to acknowledge a request while delegated work runs. As background work progresses, use [`session.commentary.append`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#keep-updates-accurate-and-useful) to provide updates you want GPT-Live to say aloud.

For backend prompts, conversation context, tool results, typed input, and API examples, read [Delegation and tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation). For the architecture overview, read [Getting started with GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live).

  return new Intl.DateTimeFormat(LOCALE[lang], {
    month: "short",
    day: "numeric",
    hour: "2-digit",
    minute: "2-digit",
  }).format(new Date(unixSecs * 1000));
}

/** "05:39", the same clock face the call view uses. */
export function formatDuration(secs: number): string {
  const m = String(Math.floor(secs / 60)).padStart(2, "0");
  const s = String(Math.floor(secs % 60)).padStart(2, "0");
  return `${m}:${s}`;
}

/** The persona's display name in the UI language, or undefined for an unmapped agent. */
export function personaName(personaId: string | undefined, lang: Lang): string | undefined {
  const p = personaId ? PERSONAS.find((x) => x.id === personaId) : undefined;
  return p ? resolvePersona(p, lang).name : undefined;
}

I've stopped before changing anything in the project, for two reasons.

**1. Installing the Archil SDK was blocked.** Running `bun add disk` in the project was refused by the auto-mode permission check, which gave no reason. Earlier I installed `disk` only in a throwaway folder. You can run it yourself with `! bun add disk`, or allow it and I'll retry.

**2. Your side agent is right: the transcripts can come from the server.** After our route creates the GPT-Live session, it can open a second, server-side connection to that session (`wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{id}/attach`) and receive both transcripts there.

| | Server captures (side connection) | Browser posts |
|---|---|---|
| Trust | Server hears it straight from OpenAI, like the ElevenLabs setup | Server must trust what the browser sends |
| Tab closed mid-call | Transcript still saved and sent to mem0 | Last part lost; a final upload on close is limited to 64 KB |
| Code | Browser only plays audio and shows captions; no save queue | Save queue plus a final upload on close |
| Catch | Connect quickly: it only replays the last 3 seconds, so a slow connect can drop the greeting's first words. The dev server holds one open connection per call | Works with any host |
| Deployment | Fine on `next dev` and on a long-running server. On serverless hosting, the function's time limit would cut off long calls | Fine anywhere |

**I recommend the server-side capture.** It keeps the rule that the server reads transcripts from the provider, and saving no longer depends on the browser tab. Since this is dev-only with no production deployment, the long-lived connection is acceptable for now. We'd revisit it if this ever moves to serverless hosting.

The rest of the plan stays the same:
- An `OPENAI LIVE` row.
- Calls stored in Archil.
- One history list combining ElevenLabs and OpenAI Live calls.
- CONTINUE on a Live call starts a new session with the earlier conversation loaded into it.
- Japanese uses harema for the female personas and shida for the male ones.
- English uses a draft cast from the GPT-Live voice list. Two picks are compromises because that list has no British feminine voice: Nova stays on `sage`, and Vesper gets `willow`, which is Irish.

To continue, I need two answers:
1. Should I switch to server-side transcript capture?
2. Will you run `! bun add disk`, or allow me to?

https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/custom-voices

I'll review the custom voices later, we can create them first

# Custom voices

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL.

Custom voices enable you to create a voice for your agent or application. Choose how to create the voice:

- **From a description:** Use prompt-to-voice to generate a voice for [GPT-Live](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live). Describe the vocal qualities you want in a text prompt.
- **From a recording:** Provide a consent recording and a short reference sample. These voices can be used with GPT-Live, the [Text to Speech API](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/audio/subresources/speech/methods/create), the [Realtime API](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/realtime), or the [Chat Completions API with audio output](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/audio-chat-completions).

To choose an existing GPT-Live voice, see [Voice options](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-conversations#voice-options).

## Create a voice from a description

Prompt-to-voice creates and saves a voice from a text description. You don't need a reference recording or a consent recording for this workflow.

Prompt-to-voice is generally available to all API customers. Prompt-generated
  voices work with GPT-Live. They aren't supported by the Text to Speech,
  Realtime, or Chat Completions APIs.

### Responsible use

- **Use voices responsibly.** Don’t impersonate others or violate our [Usage Policies](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/).
- **Use adult voices.** Children's voices aren't allowed.
- **Be transparent.** Tell listeners that the speech is AI-generated, and preserve any provenance metadata, watermarks, or other indicators of its synthetic origin.
- **Voices aren’t guaranteed to be unique.** Others may generate similar voices or output. Your output ownership rights remain governed by your Agreement with OpenAI.
- **[Terms](https://openai.com/policies/service-terms/)** apply to your and your end users’ use of prompt-to-voice.

### Create and save the voice

Create a voice through the API or in the [voice Playground](https://platform.openai.com/audio/voices/edit). Creating a prompt-generated voice is free. Using it to generate speech in GPT-Live is billed at regular session rates.

Send a JSON request to `/v1/audio/voices` with `type` set to `prompt`:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/voices \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "type": "prompt",
    "name": "Support assistant",
    "prompt": "A calm, reassuring adult voice for a customer support assistant. Speak with an American English accent, a mid-range pitch, a smooth, warm tone, and a steady, conversational pace.",
    "model": "auto"
  }' \
  -o voice.json
```


`script_hint` is an optional example script used to guide voice generation. If you leave it out, the service generates a script from your voice description. To supply your own, include up to 2,000 characters of representative speech. Blank or too-short scripts are rejected.

Each successful request creates a new saved voice. The response contains metadata, including its ID, creation time in Unix seconds, and original voice-description prompt. It doesn't include audio or a preview:

```json
{
  "object": "audio.voice",
  "id": "voice_123",
  "name": "Support assistant",
  "created_at": 0,
  "type": "prompt",
  "prompt": "A calm, reassuring adult voice for a customer support assistant. Speak with an American English accent, a mid-range pitch, a smooth, warm tone, and a steady, conversational pace."
}
```

Save the returned `id` and retain the original voice prompt. Reuse a saved voice when you want the same voice in another session. You can create up to 100 prompt-generated voices per organization. This limit also applies when your application creates voices for its customers.

### Describe the voice

Describe vocal qualities in plain language. For example:

```text
A calm, reassuring adult voice for a customer support assistant. Speak with an
American English accent, a mid-range pitch, a smooth, warm tone, and a steady,
conversational pace.
```

The following examples show qualities you can describe. These are words in your prompt, rather than separate API parameters:

| Quality         | What to describe                                          | Example wording                        |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Accent          | Regional pronunciation and accent strength                | American English, with a strong accent |
| Age             | The perceived age of the voice                            | An adult in their 30s                  |
| Presentation    | How the voice presents                                    | Feminine                               |
| Pitch           | How low or high the voice sounds                          | Mid-range pitch                        |
| Timbre          | The tone of the voice                                     | Smooth and rich                        |
| Texture         | Raspiness, hoarseness, or clarity                         | Smooth                                 |
| Loudness        | Vocal effort                                              | Moderate vocal effort                  |
| Speech rate     | How quickly the voice speaks                              | Medium pace                            |
| Distinctiveness | How pronounced the voice's individual character should be | Moderately distinctive                 |

Describe the qualities themselves. Don't request imitation of a named person, public figure, or fictional character. Children's voices aren't allowed; describe an adult voice.

### Example descriptions

Use these descriptions as starting points and listen to the results in your application.

**Calm assistant**

```text
A warm adult voice with a mid-range pitch and smooth, rich timbre.
Use moderate vocal effort and an unhurried, reassuring delivery.
```

**Lively guide**

```text
A bright, clear adult voice with a slightly higher pitch and a lightly textured timbre.
Use a lively, conversational delivery at a brisk but easy-to-follow pace.
```

Keep conversation rules, such as answer length, interruptions, and when to delegate, in your [GPT-Live session instructions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-prompting).

### Listen to the voice in GPT-Live

Listening to a voice in the Playground runs a GPT-Live session and is billed as a regular session.

Set `session.audio.output.voice.id` to the returned voice ID. For voice performance, include the original voice description in `session.instructions` alongside your application's conversation instructions.

Replace `voice_123` with the ID returned by your creation request:

```json
{
  "model": "gpt-live-1",
  "instructions": "You are a helpful voice assistant. A calm, reassuring adult voice for a customer support assistant. Speak with an American English accent, a mid-range pitch, a smooth, warm tone, and a steady, conversational pace.",
  "audio": { "output": { "voice": { "id": "voice_123" } } }
}
```

For [WebRTC](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-webrtc?api=live), include this configuration in the JSON `session` field alongside `transport`. For [WebSockets](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-websockets?api=live), include it in the first `session.start` event. Follow the connection guide to send audio and hear the voice. Choose the voice at startup; start a new session to try a different voice.

Voice creation through `/v1/audio/voices`, including creation from recordings, isn't compatible with Zero Data Retention. GPT-Live speech generations are eligible for Zero Data Retention when it's enabled for your organization or project. Stored session recordings, recording downloads, and session forking aren't available with Zero Data Retention. See the [data controls](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/data-residency#v1livesessions) for session storage and retention requirements.

### Refine and reuse

Change one quality at a time and compare the results using the same short passage and a few conversational turns. Listen for the accent, pace, and other qualities your application needs. Keep the voice ID you prefer and reuse it.

Each creation request saves a new voice. To try another saved voice, start a new GPT-Live session with its ID.

## Create a voice from a recording

To create a voice from a recording, provide a short sample audio reference that the model will seek to replicate.



    {
      "Custom voices created from recordings are limited to eligible customers. Contact our "
    }
    [{"sales team"}](https://openai.com/contact-sales/)
    {
      " to learn more. Once enabled for your organization, you’ll have access to the "
    }
    [{"Voices"}](https://platform.openai.com/audio/voices)
    {" tab under Audio."}
  






### Prepare and upload the recordings

Voices from recordings must be created through an API request. See the API reference for the full set of API operations.

Creating a voice from a recording requires two separate audio recordings:

1. **Consent recording:** This recording captures the voice actor providing consent to create a likeness of their voice. The actor must read one of the consent phrases provided below.
2. **Sample recording:** The actual audio sample that the model will try to adhere to. The voice must match the consent recording.

**Tips for creating a high-quality voice**

The quality of your custom voice is highly dependent on the quality of the sample you provide. Optimizing the recording quality can make a big difference.

- Record in a quiet space with minimal echo.
- Use a professional XLR microphone.
- Stay about 7–8 inches from the mic with a pop filter in between, and keep that distance consistent.
- The model copies exactly what you give it—tone, cadence, energy, pauses, habits—so record the exact voice you want. Be consistent in energy, style, and accent throughout.
- Small variations in the audio sample can result in quality differences with the generated voice. Try multiple examples to find the best fit.

**Requirements and limitations**

- At most 20 voices from recordings can be created per organization.
- The audio samples must be 60 seconds or less.
- The audio samples must be one of the following types: `mpeg`, `wav`, `ogg`, `aac`, `flac`, `webm`, or `mp4`.

Refer to the Text-to-Speech Supplemental Agreement for additional terms of use.

**Creating a voice consent**

The consent audio recording must only include one of the following phrases. Any divergence from the script will lead to a failure.


| Language          | Phrase                                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| German (`de`)     | Ich bin der Eigentümer dieser Stimme und bin damit einverstanden, dass OpenAI diese Stimme zur Erstellung eines synthetischen Stimmmodells verwendet. |
| English (`en`)    | I am the owner of this voice and I consent to OpenAI using this voice to create a synthetic voice model.                                              |
| Spanish (`es`)    | Soy el propietario de esta voz y doy mi consentimiento para que OpenAI la utilice para crear un modelo de voz sintética.                              |
| French (`fr`)     | Je suis le propriétaire de cette voix et j'autorise OpenAI à utiliser cette voix pour créer un modèle de voix synthétique.                            |
| Hindi (`hi`)      | मैं इस आवाज का मालिक हूं और मैं सिंथेटिक आवाज मॉडल बनाने के लिए OpenAI को इस आवाज का उपयोग करने की सहमति देता हूं                                     |
| Indonesian (`id`) | Saya adalah pemilik suara ini dan saya memberikan persetujuan kepada OpenAI untuk menggunakan suara ini guna membuat model suara sintetis.            |
| Italian (`it`)    | Sono il proprietario di questa voce e acconsento che OpenAI la utilizzi per creare un modello di voce sintetica.                                      |
| Japanese (`ja`)   | 私はこの音声の所有者であり、OpenAIがこの音声を使用して音声合成 モデルを作成することを承認します。                                                     |
| Korean (`ko`)     | 나는 이 음성의 소유자이며 OpenAI가 이 음성을 사용하여 음성 합성 모델을 생성할 것을 허용합니다.                                                        |
| Dutch (`nl`)      | Ik ben de eigenaar van deze stem en ik geef OpenAI toestemming om deze stem te gebruiken om een synthetisch stemmodel te maken.                       |
| Polish (`pl`)     | Jestem właścicielem tego głosu i wyrażam zgodę na wykorzystanie go przez OpenAI w celu utworzenia syntetycznego modelu głosu.                         |
| Portuguese (`pt`) | Eu sou o proprietário desta voz e autorizo o OpenAI a usá-la para criar um modelo de voz sintética.                                                   |
| Russian (`ru`)    | Я являюсь владельцем этого голоса и даю согласие OpenAI на использование этого голоса для создания модели синтетического голоса.                      |
| Ukrainian (`uk`)  | Я є власником цього голосу і даю згоду OpenAI використовувати цей голос для створення синтетичної голосової моделі.                                   |
| Vietnamese (`vi`) | Tôi là chủ sở hữu giọng nói này và tôi đồng ý cho OpenAI sử dụng giọng nói này để tạo mô hình giọng nói tổng hợp.                                     |
| Chinese (`zh`)    | 我是此声音的拥有者并授权OpenAI使用此声音创建语音合成模型                                                                                              |

Then upload the recording via the API. A successful upload will return the consent recording ID that you’ll reference later. Note the consent can be used for multiple different voice creations if the same voice actor is making multiple attempts.

```bash
curl https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/voice_consents \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -F "name=test_consent" \
  -F "language=en" \
  -F "recording=@$HOME/tmp/voice_consent/consent_recording.wav;type=audio/x-wav"
```


**Creating a voice**

Next, you’ll create the actual voice by referencing the consent recording ID, and providing the voice sample.

```bash
curl https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/voices \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -F "name=test_voice" \
  -F "audio_sample=@$HOME/tmp/voice_consent/audio_sample_recording.wav;type=audio/x-wav" \
  -F "consent=cons_123abc"
```


If successful, the created voice will be listed under the [Audio tab](https://platform.openai.com/audio/voices).





## Using a voice from a recording during speech generation

Use `gpt-realtime-2.1-mini` with the [Realtime API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime) to generate speech in your custom voice. Set `session.audio.output.voice` to an object containing the voice ID before the session's first audio response.

**Configure the Realtime session**

Use the following request body when [creating a Realtime client secret](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/realtime/subresources/client_secrets/methods/create), then follow the [WebRTC connection guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-webrtc?api=realtime) to connect with that secret. Replace `voice_123abc` with the ID returned by your voice creation request:

```typescript
const sessionConfig = JSON.stringify({
  session: {
    type: "realtime",
    model: "gpt-realtime-2.1-mini",
    instructions: "Read the user's text aloud without adding commentary.",
    output_modalities: ["audio"],
    audio: {
      output: {
        voice: { id: "voice_123abc" },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

```go
sessionConfig := map[string]any{
	"session": map[string]any{
		"type":              "realtime",
		"model":             "gpt-realtime-2.1-mini",
		"instructions":      "Read the user's text aloud without adding commentary.",
		"output_modalities": []string{"audio"},
		"audio":             map[string]any{"output": map[string]any{"voice": map[string]any{"id": "voice_123abc"}}},
	},
}
```

```ruby
# Replace the illustrative IDs and URLs below with your own resource values.
require "json"

session_config = JSON.generate(
  session: {
    type: "realtime",
    model: "gpt-realtime-2.1-mini",
    instructions: "Read the user's text aloud without adding commentary.",
    output_modalities: ["audio"],
    audio: { output: { voice: { id: "voice_123abc" } } }
  }
)
puts(session_config)
```


For text-to-speech generation, [add a user message containing the text](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations#text-inputs-and-outputs), then send `response.create` with `output_modalities` set to `["audio"]`. The session instructions ask the model to read the supplied text aloud. Receive the generated audio through the WebRTC audio track, as described in [Handling audio with WebRTC](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations#handling-audio-with-webrtc).





## Use a voice from a recording with GPT-Live

Use a project-scoped API key approved for both GPT-Live and custom voice
creation. Reading consent phrases and using a custom voice require
`api.voices.read`; creating consents and voices requires `api.voices.write` and
custom-voice API access. Use the same project for every request and keep the API
key on a trusted server.

### Prepare the recordings

List the current supported consent phrases before recording:

```bash
curl https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/consent_phrases \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

The consent recording and reference sample must come from the same person. The
sample needs at least five seconds of actual speech and at least 15 transcribed
text tokens; silence does not count. Use a 10–60-second
recording with several complete sentences. Each upload is limited to 10 MiB.
The service extracts the reference transcript from your recording.

Browser recorders may label audio `audio/webm;codecs=opus`, which the upload
endpoint rejects. When constructing an upload, use the supported base MIME type
`audio/webm` while preserving the original audio bytes. Use the consent and voice
creation requests above, then save the returned voice ID.

### Select the voice at session creation

Pass a custom voice as an object, such as `{ "id": "voice_123" }`. Named voices
such as `"marin"` use strings.

`gpt-live-1` supports custom voices with English accents. To use an accent, also
specify it in `session.instructions`, such as "Speak British English" or "Speak
Irish English." The example below uses British English; change the instruction
to match the accent you want for your custom voice.

Include the following configuration in the initial session:

```json
{
  "model": "gpt-live-1",
  "instructions": "You are a helpful voice assistant. Speak British English.",
  "audio": { "output": { "voice": { "id": "voice_123" } } }
}
```

For [WebRTC](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-webrtc?api=live), have your application server
place this configuration in the JSON `session` field alongside `transport`.
Authenticate requests to your server with application credentials, and keep the
OpenAI API key on the server.

For [WebSockets](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/voice-websockets?api=live), put the configuration
in the first `session.start` event. Follow the connection guide for streaming
audio and closing the session.

### Handle access and lifecycle failures

- Choose the voice at session creation. Start a new session to use a different voice.
- A deleted or revoked voice, a consent from another project, or missing custom-voice access can appear as a `404`.
- Malformed audio, a mismatched speaker, or a non-project-scoped key is rejected.

Confirm your project's permissions, recording minimums, and upload limits
before creating a voice. See [GPT-Live getting started](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live)
for session setup requirements.

I'm blocked on two things that only you can fix. I've written two files so far.

**2. The OpenAI key can't create voices.** Creating the first custom voice failed with `401 … Missing scopes: api.voices.write`. Please add the **Voices → Write** permission to the key on the OpenAI dashboard (it's a restricted key). Then run:
```
! fnox exec -- bun scripts/openai-live/create-voices.ts
```
It creates the five voices and writes each voice's id back into the config file. If you rerun it, it skips voices that already have an id. Creating them is free. You can also create them in the voice Playground and paste the ids into the config yourself.

**The two files:**
- `config/openai-live-voices.json` holds the voice for each persona and language, and the app will read it. Where a custom voice has no id yet, it uses the listed built-in voice instead.

  | Cipher | vesper | **custom** (falls back to shida) |
  | Vesper | willow | harema |

**3. Please confirm where transcripts come from.** You allowed `bun add` but didn't answer this one. I'll go with **server-side capture** unless you say otherwise: the server opens its own connection to each GPT-Live session, then saves the transcript to Archil and sends it to mem0 when the call ends.

<result>// Conversation history: the visitor's finished ElevenLabs calls, newest first.
//
// POST { userId, cursor? } → { items, nextCursor }. POST rather than GET keeps
// the visitor id out of URLs and logs. Dev only: ELEVENLABS_API_KEY from fnox.

import { listConversations } from "@/lib/conversations/elevenlabs-history";
import { fail, parseHistoryRequest, upstreamFailure } from "@/lib/conversations/route-helpers";

export const runtime = "nodejs";
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";

// ElevenLabs cursors are opaque tokens; bound them so nothing odd reaches the URL.
const CURSOR_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9_\-=.]{1,512}$/;

export async function POST(req: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const parsed = await parseHistoryRequest(req);
  if (!parsed.ok) return parsed.response;
  const { cursor } = parsed.body;
  if (cursor !== undefined && (typeof cursor !== "string" || !CURSOR_RE.test(cursor))) {
    return fail("cursor is malformed.", 400);
  }
  try {
    return Response.json(await listConversations(parsed.apiKey, parsed.userId, cursor));
  } catch (err) {
    return upstreamFailure(err);
  }
}
</result>
</event>

content.text:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.


Summary:
**1. Primary Request and Intent**

Build OpenAI conversation history plus mem0 memory on GPT-Live (gpt-live-1) as a new "OPENAI LIVE" provider row. The user's decisions, in order:
- (1) Add an "OPENAI LIVE" row for gpt-live-1.
- (2) Originally, transcripts come from the browser. After the side agent's note, I recommended server-side sideband capture and am proceeding with it; the user did not object.
- (3) Store transcripts on the Archil disk "realtime-persona" (ID `dsk-000000000013d2cc`, region `aws-us-west-2`, baseUrl `https://control.green.us-west-2.aws.prod.archil.com`, s3BaseUrl `https://s3.green.us-west-2.aws.prod.archil.com`). It is mounted at `/Volumes/realtime-persona/`, and `ARCHIL_API_KEY` is in fnox.
- (4) Japanese uses harema (feminine) and shida (masculine) by gender; English uses the GPT-Live voice options.

Later instruction: "For Nova in English, and Japanese personas other than vesper and aria, and onyx, we can use custom voice from text description … I'll review the custom voices later, we can create them first."
- Custom voices: nova-en, sage-ja, nova-ja, echo-ja, cipher-ja.
- Vesper and Aria JA use harema; Onyx JA uses shida.

Archil guide rules, preserved verbatim:
- "Credentials come from `$ARCHIL_API_KEY`. They're left out of this prompt on purpose. If they aren't set, ask me for them. Never print, log, or write them to a file."
- "Ask me before changing anything these steps don't cover."

**2. Key Technical Concepts**

GPT-Live (gpt-live-1):
- The server creates the session with `POST /v1/live/sessions` and the body `{session:{model,instructions,input,audio:{output:{voice}},delegation:{type:"client"}}, transport:{type:"webrtc",sdp}}`. The response is `{session:{id}, transport:{sdp}}`. There is no ephemeral token, and creation bills 15 s up front.
- The browser must wait for ICE gathering to complete before posting the offer (the answer is ice-lite).
- Data channel "oai-events" events:
  - `session.started`
  - `session.input_transcript.delta` / `session.output_transcript.delta` with `{delta, start_ms, end_ms}`
  - `session.delegation.created` with `{delegation:{id}}`
  - `session.closed` with `{reason}`
  - `error`
- Client commands: `session.instructions.append`, `session.thinking.append` and `session.commentary.append`, each `{event_id, delegation_id: null|id, content ≤500 tokens}`; `session.close`; `session.input_audio.mute`/`unmute`.
- There is no response.done, response.cancel or turn ids.
- Sideband: `wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{id}/attach` with an Authorization header. It replays the last 3 s and receives transcripts plus reflected audio (`session.input_audio.append`, `session.output_audio.delta`). Verified working from Node with `new WebSocket(url, {headers:{Authorization}})`.
- Limits:
  - startup `input`: ≤128 messages, ≤8,192 tokens; roles developer/user/assistant; `input_text`/`output_text`
  - `instructions`: ≤16,384 tokens
- GPT-Live summarizes at 90% of its 128k context.
- Prompt template headings: "Backchannel policy", "Interruption policy", "Delegation policy" with "Backend tools", "Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when", "Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when".
- Greeting: a developer message in the input, plus `session.instructions.append` after `session.started` (instructions is the exact-wording channel).
- Custom voices:
  - created with `POST /v1/audio/voices` `{type:"prompt", name, prompt, model:"auto", script_hint?}`
  - used as `audio.output.voice: {id}`
  - include the voice description in the instructions
  - need key scope `api.voices.write`
- Built-in Live voices (38): alloy, ash, ballad, beacon, bossa, brise, calandria, cedar, cinder, compas, coral, delta, destello, echo, flitz, gleam, halo, harema, hornero, juni, luciernaga, marin, meridian, nira, noeul, nuri, pearl, quartz, ripple, sage, shida, shimmer, sillage, stone, tempo, verse, vesper, willow. An unknown voice returns a misleading 403 "Voice session access denied".

Archil SDK (`disk` package):
- `archil.configure({apiKey, region, baseUrl, s3BaseUrl})`, then `getDisk(id)`.
- `putObject(key, body, contentType|opts)`, `getObject(key)` returning a Uint8Array, `headObject`, `objectExists`, `deleteObject`.
- `listObjects(prefix, {recursive, singlePage, limit, continuationToken, startAfter})` returns `{objects:[{key,size,lastModified}], isTruncated, nextContinuationToken}`.
- Errors are `ArchilS3Error` with status and code.

Project conventions (AGENTS.md):
- bun, oxlint, oxfmt; Next 16; React 19.
- Gates: `bunx tsc --noEmit` → `bun run lint` → `bun run fmt:check` → `bun run build`.
- Every user-facing change is bilingual: `STRINGS.en`/`ja` in `lib/i18n.ts`, and `CAPTION_KEYS` for engine sentinel captions.
- `setTurns` updaters must be pure.
- Per-start attempt tokens.
- The `rg` shell command is blocked by a hook for TS files; use `tools.Grep` or ast-grep.
- Use `fnox exec --` from the repo root for secrets.

Rejected approach: the mem0 voice-companion cookbook (Python chained VoicePipeline). Use the companion pattern instead (recall before, add after; optionally `custom_instructions`/categories).

**3. Files and Code Sections**

Read for context:
- `lib/memory/*`: call-lifecycle, mem0-rest (`addMemories(apiKey,userId,messages,metadata,timestamp)`, `listRecentMemories(apiKey,userId,limit)`, `mem0ApiKey()`, `Mem0Error`), framing (`formatMemoryUpdate(memories, lang)`), client, ids, user-id, elevenlabs-conversation (`ConversationError(message,status)`).
- `app/api/memory/{ingest,recall}/route.ts`
- `lib/conversations/{types,client,resume,elevenlabs-history,route-helpers}.ts`
- `hooks/{use-resume,use-conversations,use-session-routing}.ts`
- `lib/realtime/{use-realtime-session,types,openai-agent,use-openai-session,japanese,realtime-model-config}.ts`
- `lib/data.ts`, `lib/i18n.ts` (501 lines; CAPTION_KEYS near the end)
- `components/tsubaki/{app-shell,routing-notice,providers-view,personas-view,conversations-view,conversation-list,conversation-detail,conversation-format}.tsx`
- `app/globals.css`: `.tb-ja-mark` at about line 2109, `.tb-ja-mark-agent`, `.tb-ja-mark-prompt` (dashed), another reference near line 2260
- `fnox.toml`: already has an `ARCHIL_API_KEY` entry
- `next.config.ts`

Created or modified so far:
- `config/openai-live-voices.json` (created). Each persona has `{en,ja}` entries of the form `{voice, custom?:{name,prompt,scriptHint,id:null}}`.

  | Persona | English | Japanese |
  |---|---|---|
  | aria | gleam | harema |
  | onyx | cedar | shida |
  | sage | meridian | shida + custom `tsubaki-sage-ja` |
  | nova | sage + custom `tsubaki-nova-en` | harema + custom `tsubaki-nova-ja` |
  | echo | marin | harema + custom `tsubaki-echo-ja` |
  | cipher | vesper | shida + custom `tsubaki-cipher-ja` |
  | vesper | willow | harema |

  The descriptions follow persona pitch, accent and temperament; the JA voices say "native standard Japanese with a Tokyo accent". All ids are still null.
- `scripts/openai-live/create-voices.ts` (created). It is idempotent, creates customs without an id through `/v1/audio/voices`, and writes each id back after every voice. Usage: `fnox exec -- bun scripts/openai-live/create-voices.ts`. It failed with 401 for missing `api.voices.write`.
- `config/realtime-models.json`: now `{openai:{model:"gpt-realtime-2.1",transcriptionModel:"gpt-realtime-whisper"}, openaiLive:{model:"gpt-live-1"}, elevenlabs:{ttsModel:{en,ja:"eleven_v4_turbo"}}}`.
- `config/archil.json`: `{"$comment", diskId, region, baseUrl, s3BaseUrl, root:"tsubaki"}`.
- `lib/realtime/realtime-model-config.ts`: added `export const OPENAI_LIVE_MODEL: string = catalog.openaiLive.model;`.
- `lib/realtime/openai-live-voices.ts`:

  - makes `callId = newLiveCallId()` (`olc_<32 hex>`);
  - in parallel: mem0 recall with a 2 s cap, resume load from Archil with a 3 s cap and an ownership check by userId path, and creation of the Archil record;

  - creates the Live session;
  - starts the sideband capture;
  - returns `{sdp, callId, greeting}`.

Brutalist/editorial voice console for talking to seven personas (aspects of one camellia spirit) over seven interchangeable realtime transports. The whole console, voice and UI, runs in **English or Japanese** from a single switch.

### Long-term memory (`lib/memory/`)

mem0 gives the ElevenLabs engine a memory of the visitor across calls. Other engines don't use it yet. It is the live `memory.recall` tool (`lib/data.ts`; the other tools are still `preview` mocks): turning it off in Settings skips both recall and ingest.

- **Shared, not per persona.** Memory is scoped by mem0 `user_id` only, and persona, language and source go in metadata. That fits the fiction (seven aspects of one spirit), and it avoids a mem0 trap: an AND of `user_id` + `agent_id` returns nothing, because mem0 stores the entities separately.
- **Ident

voice:
**Voice.** Each transport speaks Japanese at its own level (`Provider.ja`):
- `agent` (ElevenLabs): a dedicated JA platform agent per persona (`tsubaki-<id>-ja`, `PERSONA_AGENT_IDS_JA`), with its own JA prompt and a cast native-speaker voice.
- `prompt` (xAI, OpenAI, Gemini): none of these sessions has a language parameter. `localizeAgent` (`lib/realtime/japanese.ts`) appends a language rule to the English persona prompt and swaps the opening direction for the persona's `ja.greet`. The voice stays the same.
- none (cascade, fal, KYUTAI): no Japanese path. Voxtral TTS has no Japanese and PersonaPlex is English-only. Don't fake one; set `ja` on the provider row only once the engine really speaks it.

**Routing** (`hooks/use-session-routing.ts`):
- Japanese picked on a no-path transport fails over to the last transport a Japanese session ran on, else the best available (`agent` before `prompt`).
- A no-path transport picked while Japanese is on drops the language to EN.
- Any transport or language change during a call ends it and opens a new session; nothing is handed over mid-call. `routing-notice.tsx` explains each re-route.

### Conversation history (`lib/conversations/`)

The CONVERSATIONS section (key H) lists the visitor's stored ElevenLabs calls and reads one back; CONTINUE lets the next call pick it up.

- **ElevenLabs is the store.** `/api/conversations` lists by the visitor's `user_id` (finished calls where they spoke), and `/api/conversations/[id]` returns one transcript only if its `user_id` matches; otherwise it answers 404, like a missing call. Persona and language come from the agent id (`agentPersona` in `elevenlabs-agent.ts`), not from the agent name.
- **Continuing is replay, not resume.** ElevenLabs has no way to reopen a conversation. CONTINUE selects the call's persona, routes to ELEVENLABS in the call's language (`routeTo`), and arms it (`hooks/use-resume.ts`). At connect, the tail of the old transcript goes to the agent as an in-world contextual update (`resume.ts`, EN and JA, last 40 turns). The agent's static first message still plays first; overriding it would need `platform_settings.overrides` on all 14 agents.
- **Armed only where it can run:** on the ELEVENLABS row with the call's own persona. A continued call that ends spends the target, except when routing replaced it mid-call (a language change); the replacement continues the same conversation.
- **Other transports can't read these calls.** xAI and OpenAI could seed a session with `conversation.item.create`, and Gemini with `clientContent` turns, but none of that is wired; continuing elsewhere is pending.
- *Local check:* continue a stored call, press CALL, and ask what you were talking about. The persona should answer from the old call without reading it back.



fenced:
- **Per-start attempt tokens:** a language change mid-call hangs up and restarts the *same* hook. A shared `endedRef` boolean alone lets leftover setup from the old call resume into the new one, because the new `start()` resets it to `false`.
  - **Fenced:** xAI, OpenAI and Gemini give each `start()` its own token (`attemptRef` + `ended()`), checked by every async continuation.
  - **Not fenced yet:** fal and KYUTAI still rely on a shared `endedRef`, and the cascade has no per-start guard. Routing never restarts them in place, because they have no Japanese path and any route change moves the session to another hook. A fast manual hang-up → CALL could still hit the race.
  - Add the token before giving an engine a Japanese path, and in any new engine.

/** The engine that can continue a call from this store. */
export const SOURCE_ENGINE: Record<HistorySource, NonNullable<Provider["engine"]>> = {
  elevenlabs: "elevenlabs",
  "openai-live": "openai-live",
};

export function useResume(provider: Provider, persona: Persona): ResumeState {
  const [target, setTarget] = useState<ConversationDetail | null>(null);
  const armed =
    target && provider.engine === SOURCE_ENGINE[target.source] && target.personaId === persona.id
      ? target
      : null;
  return { target, armed, select: setTarget, clear: () => setTarget(null) };
}

export function useSpendResumeAfterCall(
  resume: ResumeState,
  callState: CallState,
  restartPending: boolean,
): void {
  const { armed, clear } = resume;
  const clearRef = useRef(clear);
  clearRef.current = clear;
  // Whether the call in progress (or the one just replaced) continued the
  // target. Set only once it connected: a call that fails to connect leaves the
  // target armed for another try.
  const continuingRef = useRef(false);
  const live = isLive(callState);
  const connected = live && callState !== "connecting";
  useEffect(() => {
    if (live) {
      if (connected) continuingRef.current ||= armed !== null;
      return;
    }
    if (continuingRef.current && !restartPending) {
      continuingRef.current = false;
      clearRef.current();
    }
  }, [live, connected, armed, restartPending]);
}

input.new_string:
The CONVERSATIONS section (key H) lists the visitor's stored ElevenLabs and OPENAI LIVE calls in one list and reads one back; CONTINUE lets the next call pick it up on the transport that stored it.

- **Two stores, one list.** `lib/conversations/history.ts` merges them newest first; the paging cursor (`history-cursor.ts`) carries both stores' positions. Either key alone (`ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`, `ARCHIL_API_KEY`) lists its own calls. The detail route dispatches on the id: `conv_…` is ElevenLabs, `olc_…` is OPENAI LIVE.
- **ElevenLabs stores its own calls.**

- **OPENAI LIVE calls are ours to store.** GPT-Live keeps no transcripts we can read back, so `/api/openai-live/session` creates the session server-side, then attaches a sideband WebSocket (`…/live/sessions/{id}/attach`) that hears the same transcript deltas (`live-capture.ts`). The record goes to the Archil disk (`config/archil.json`, `lib/storage/archil.ts`, `live-store.ts`) at `tsubaki/openai-live/calls/<userId>/<callId>.json`, checkpointed every 10 s and finalized at `session.closed`, which is also when mem0 ingests it (`lib/memory/live-ingest.ts`). An index of empty markers (`index/<userId>/<inverted start>_<callId>`) lists newest first without reading records.
  - Archil's S3 listing **ignores `start-after`**, so `listIndex` skips past the cursor itself. Archil also keeps **directory markers**: delete a directory's files before the directory.
  - Captures live in the dev server process. Restarting it mid-call loses the tail since the last checkpoint; the record then lists as abandoned after 15 minutes.
  - Startup seeding (`live-seed.ts`): recalled memories, then as much of a continued call as fits (newest turns kept), then the greeting, all within GPT-Live's 128-message / 8,192-token `input` cap.
- **Other transports can't read these calls.**

- `voice` (OPENAI LIVE): Japanese through the instructions like `prompt`, but spoken by a native voice cast per persona (`config/openai-live-voices.json`): harema (feminine), shida (masculine), or a custom voice made from a text description by `scripts/openai-live/create-voices.ts` (needs the `api.voices.write` key scope). Until a custom voice has an id, the built-in voice speaks.
- `prompt` (xAI, OpenAI, Gemini):
else the best available (`agent`, then `voice`, then `prompt`).

- **OPENAI LIVE is full duplex.** No half-duplex mic gating; Chrome's echo canceller does the work, with the same direct `<audio>` playback as OPENAI. GPT-Live has no response or turn events: turns are grouped by delta timing (`live-transcript.ts`) and "speaking" follows the output level. An unknown voice fails session creation with a misleading 403 "Voice session access denied".
  - *Local check:* a call on laptop speakers must not produce phantom user turns; talk over the agent and it should yield.
- **Gemini** output is fixed at 24 kHz,

ElevenLabs calls remember the visitor across sessions, through
[mem0](https://docs.mem0.ai). Memory is shared by all seven personas: they are
aspects of one spirit, so any of them may recall what you told another. The
persona and language of each call are kept as mem0 metadata.

   never blocks a call.
2. **Ingest.** On hangup the browser posts the conversation id to
   `POST /api/memory/ingest`. The server waits for ElevenLabs to finish the
   conversation, checks that it belongs to you, and sends its spoken turns to
   mem0, which extracts the facts asynchronously.

Your identity is an opaque `tsubaki-<uuid>` in localStorage

without memory. Memory is the `memory.recall` tool in Settings; turning it off

## Wiring the real OpenAI provider

OpenAI's realtime API (`gpt-realtime-2.1`) connects over **WebRTC** — the browser's
peer connection carries the audio both ways, so there's no hand-rolled PCM
pipeline. A short-lived **ephemeral key** is minted server-side at
`POST /api/openai/token`; the browser then POSTs its SDP offer straight to
`https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls` with that key, and session control +
transcripts flow over the `oai-events` data channel. The secret `OPENAI_API_KEY`
never reaches the client.

Keep `OPENAI_API_KEY` in **fnox** and run via `fnox exec -- bun run dev`. No
`OPENAI_*` values live in `.env` files.

Per-persona config (voice, multi-line instructions, opening line, reasoning
effort, turn-detection) lives in the typed module **`lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts`**
— a shared `BASE` (model / reasoning / `gpt-realtime-whisper` input transcription /
turn-detection) plus a per-persona map of OpenAI voice + prompt + greeting,
resolved by `resolveOpenaiAgent(personaId)`. The model ids themselves live in
**`config/realtime-models.json`** (read by `lib/realtime/realtime-model-config.ts`),
the single source shared by the agent `BASE`, the `/api/openai/token` mint route,
and the Providers UI label — bump the model there and every consumer follows. The persona `instructions` follow a
light slice of OpenAI's Realtime 2.0 prompt skeleton (Role, Personality & Tone,
Pacing, Unclear Audio, Variety).

Pick the **OPENAI** row under Providers, choose a persona, and press CALL — it
mints a key, negotiates WebRTC, plays the agent's audio, shows the user + agent
transcripts (whisper for input), and barges in on server-VAD speech detection.

---
name: archil-store-gotchas
description: Archil disk (disk SDK) quirks hit while storing OPENAI LIVE transcripts — start-after ignored, directory markers, Turbopack bundling
metadata:
  type: project
---

Archil disk "realtime-persona" (config/archil.json) stores OPENAI LIVE call records via the `disk` SDK.

- S3 ListObjectsV2 ignores `start-after` (seen 2026-11-19); `listObjects({limit})` just truncates from the start. Page by skipping keys client-side (lib/conversations/live-store.ts listIndex).
- It keeps directory markers (`…/dir/`); deleting a non-empty dir marker fails 400 InvalidRequest. Delete files first, then markers.
- Turbopack can't bundle `disk` ("expression is too dynamic"): it is in next.config.ts serverExternalPackages.

**Why:** these cost a debugging round each. **How to apply:** any new Archil listing/cleanup code. Related: [[gpt-live-api-facts]].
